"an excellent spirit {was} in him"

Here, an excellent spirit represents “exceptional character and ability.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he had outstanding character and ability]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 6:4 (#1)
content:
עִלָּ֛ה לְ⁠הַשְׁכָּחָ֥ה לְ⁠דָנִיֵּ֖אל

"to find an occasion against Daniel"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of occasion, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to find some way to accuse Daniel]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 6:4 (#2)
content:
כָּ⁠ל־קֳבֵל֙ דִּֽי

"all before that"

Daniel is using all before that as a common expression of the culture to mean “because.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:4 (#3)
content:
לָ֥א הִשְׁתְּכַ֖חַת עֲלֽוֹ⁠הִי

"was not found in him"

The expression was not found in him is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they did not find in him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:5 (#1)
content:
אָֽמְרִ֔ין דִּ֣י

"were saying that"

Here, the word that introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Daniel 6:5 (#2)
content:
לָ֧א נְהַשְׁכַּ֛ח לְ⁠דָנִיֵּ֥אל דְּנָ֖ה כָּל־עִלָּ֑א לָהֵ֕ן הַשְׁכַּ֥חְנָֽה עֲל֖וֹ⁠הִי

"We will not find any occasion against this Daniel unless we find {something} against him"

If it would appear in your language that these men were making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [The only occasion we will find against this Daniel will be something]

See: Connect — Exception Clauses

title: Daniel 6:6 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠עָלְמִ֥ין חֱיִֽי

"live to eternities"

The officials are using live to eternities as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you live a very long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you live long]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:7 (#1)
content:
יִבְעֵ֣ה בָ֠עוּ

"petitions a petition"

The officials are using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root, petitions a petition. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

See: Poetry

title: Daniel 6:7 (#2)
content:
יִתְרְמֵ֕א לְ⁠גֹ֖ב אַרְיָוָתָֽ⁠א

"shall be thrown into a den of lions"

The expression shall be thrown into a den of lions is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is someone whom your servants shall throw into a den of lions]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:8 (#1)
content:
דִּי־לָ֥א תֶעְדֵּֽא

"which does not pass away"

The officials are using which does not pass away as a common expression of the culture to mean “which cannot be revoked.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [which is without end]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:9 (#1)
content:
כָּ⁠ל־קֳבֵ֖ל דְּנָ֑ה

"All before this"

Daniel is using All before this as a common expression of the culture to mean “so” or “therefore.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So then] or [Therefore]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:10 (#1)
content:
רְשִׁ֤ים כְּתָבָ⁠א֙

"the writing had been signed"

The expression the writing had been signed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the king had signed the writing]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כַוִּ֨ין פְּתִיחָ֥ן לֵ⁠הּ֙ בְּ⁠עִלִּיתֵ֔⁠הּ נֶ֖גֶד יְרוּשְׁלֶ֑ם

"now the windows to him in his upper chamber were opened toward Jerusalem"

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Daniel 6:10 (#3)
content:
כָּ⁠ל־קֳבֵל֙ דִּֽי

"all before that"

Daniel is using all before that as a common expression of the culture to mean “just as.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [just as] or [in the same way as]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:12 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠לָ֧א אֱסָ֣ר רְשַׁ֗מְתָּ דִּ֣י כָל־אֱנָ֡שׁ דִּֽי־יִבְעֵה֩ מִן־כָּל־אֱלָ֨הּ וֶֽ⁠אֱנָ֜שׁ עַד & תְּלָתִ֗ין & מִנָּ֣⁠ךְ מַלְכָּ֔⁠א יִתְרְמֵ֕א לְ⁠ג֖וֹב אַרְיָותָ֑⁠א

"Did you not sign a decree that any man who petitions from any god or man for thirty & from you, O king, shall be thrown into a den of lions"

The men are using the question form to remind the king of a decree he already made, implying that he must enforce it. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You signed a decree that any man who petitions from any god or man for thirty days, except from you, O king, shall be thrown into a den of lions!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Daniel 6:12 (#2)
content:
יִתְרְמֵ֕א לְ⁠ג֖וֹב אַרְיָותָ֑⁠א

"shall be thrown into a den of lions"

The expression shall be thrown into a den of lions is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language.

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:13 (#1)
content:
בְּנֵ֨י גָלוּתָ֜⁠א דִּ֣י יְה֗וּד

"the sons of the captivity of Judah"

The officials are using the sons of the captivity of Judah as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people who were taken away from Judah as captives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who were taken away from Judah as captives]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:13 (#2)
content:
לָא־שָׂ֨ם עלי⁠ך מַלְכָּ⁠א֙ טְעֵ֔ם

"does not set regard on you, O king"

The officials are using does not set regard on you as a common expression of the culture to mean “pays no attention to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [does not respect you] or [does not obey you]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עַ֧ל דָּנִיֵּ֛אל שָׂ֥ם בָּ֖ל לְ⁠שֵׁיזָבוּתֵ֑⁠הּ

"and he set his heart on Daniel to deliver him"

The author is using he set his heart on Daniel to deliver him as a common expression of the culture to mean “the king was determined to rescue Daniel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he resolved to rescue Daniel]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:16 (#1)
content:
בֵּ⁠אדַ֜יִן מַלְכָּ֣⁠א אֲמַ֗ר וְ⁠הַיְתִיו֙ לְ⁠דָ֣נִיֵּ֔אל וּ⁠רְמ֕וֹ לְ⁠גֻבָּ֖⁠א דִּ֣י אַרְיָוָתָ֑⁠א עָנֵ֤ה מַלְכָּ⁠א֙ וְ⁠אָמַ֣ר לְ⁠דָנִיֵּ֔אל אֱלָהָ֗⁠ךְ דִּ֣י אנתה פָּֽלַֽח־לֵ⁠הּ֙ בִּ⁠תְדִירָ֔⁠א ה֖וּא יְשֵׁיזְבִנָּֽ⁠ךְ

"Then the king was speaking, and they brought Daniel and threw {him} into a den of lions. The king answered and was saying to Daniel, “Your God, whom you are serving him in continuance, he, may he deliver you"

You could put the information about the king speaking to Daniel before the information that they threw Daniel into the den of lions. The UST models one way to do that.

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 6:16 (#2)
content:
דִּ֣י אנתה פָּֽלַֽח־לֵ⁠הּ֙

"whom you are serving him"

It might seem that the expression whom you are serving him contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [whom you are serving]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Daniel 6:17 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵיתָ֨יִת֙ אֶ֣בֶן חֲדָ֔ה וְ⁠שֻׂמַ֖ת עַל־פֻּ֣ם גֻּבָּ֑⁠א

"And a stone was brought and set over the mouth of the den"

The expression a stone was brought and set over the mouth of the den is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And servants brought a stone and set it over the mouth of the den]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:18 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שִׁנְתֵּ֖⁠הּ נַדַּ֥ת עֲלֽוֹ⁠הִי

"and his sleep departed from him"

The author is speaking of his sleep as if it were a living thing that could depart from the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he was unable to sleep]

See: Personification

title: Daniel 6:21 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠עָלְמִ֥ין חֱיִֽי

"live to eternities"

Daniel is using live to eternities as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you live a very long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you live long]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:22 (#1)
content:
קָֽדָמ֨וֹ⁠הִי֙ זָכוּ֙ הִשְׁתְּכַ֣חַת לִ֔⁠י

"innocence was found to me before him"

The expression innocence was found to me before him is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he found me to be innocent]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:22 (#2)
content:
כָּ⁠ל־קֳבֵ֗ל דִּ֤י

"all before that"

Daniel is using all before that as a common expression of the culture to mean “because.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:23 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֻסַּ֨ק דָּנִיֵּ֜אל מִן־גֻּבָּ֗⁠א

"And Daniel was brought up from the den"

The expression Daniel was brought up from the den is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the king’s servants brought Daniel up from the den]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:23 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־חֲבָל֙ לָא־הִשְׁתְּכַ֣ח בֵּ֔⁠הּ

"and any harm was not found in him"

The expression any harm was not found in him is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they found no harm in him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:24 (#1)
content:
דִּֽי־אֲכַ֤לוּ קַרְצ֨וֹ⁠הִי֙ דִּ֣י דָֽנִיֵּ֔אל

"who had eaten the pieces of Daniel"

The author is using who had eaten the pieces of Daniel as a common expression of the culture to mean “who had maliciously accused Daniel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who had maliciously accused Daniel]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:25 (#1)
content:
כְּ֠תַב לְֽ⁠כָל־עַֽמְמַיָּ֞⁠א אֻמַיָּ֧⁠א וְ⁠לִשָּׁנַיָּ֛⁠א דִּֽי־דארין בְּ⁠כָל־אַרְעָ֖⁠א שְׁלָמְ⁠כ֥וֹן יִשְׂגֵּֽא

"wrote to all of the peoples, nations, and languages that were dwelling in all of the earth, “May your peace abound"

The quotation of the letter from King Darius may begin with to all of the peoples rather than with May your peace abound. (Compare the start of the letter from King Nebuchadnezzar in 4:1.) Alternate translation: [wrote, “To all of the peoples, nations, and languages that are dwelling in all of the earth, may your peace abound”]

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Daniel 6:25 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לִשָּׁנַיָּ֛⁠א

"and languages"

Here, languages represents “the people who speak those languages.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and speakers of different languages]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 6:25 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠כָל־אַרְעָ֖⁠א

"in all of the earth"

The author says in all of the earth as an extreme statement for emphasis. The people addressed lived throughout the king’s empire. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [throughout the entire empire]

See: Hyperbole

title: Daniel 6:25 (#4)
content:
שְׁלָמְ⁠כ֥וֹן יִשְׂגֵּֽא

"May your peace abound"

The king is using May your peace abound as a common expression of the culture to mean “I wish you great well-being.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you prosper greatly]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:26 (#1)
content:
מִן־קֳדָמַ⁠י֮ שִׂ֣ים טְעֵם֒

"From before me a decree is set"

The expression From before me a decree is set is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I am making this decree]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:26 (#2)
content:
זאעין וְ⁠דָ֣חֲלִ֔ין

"trembling and fearing"

The terms trembling and fearing mean similar things. The king is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [deeply afraid]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 6:26 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠קַיָּם֙ לְ⁠עָ֣לְמִ֔ין

"and enduring to eternities"

The king is using enduring to eternities as a common expression of the culture to mean “existing forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he exists forever]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 6:26 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠מַלְכוּתֵ⁠הּ֙ דִּֽי־לָ֣א תִתְחַבַּ֔ל וְ⁠שָׁלְטָנֵ֖⁠הּ עַד־סוֹפָֽ⁠א

"and his kingdom {is one} that will not be destroyed, and his dominion {will be} to the end"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and his kingdom and his rule will never come to an end]

See: Parallelism

title: Daniel 6:26 (#5)
content:
לָ֣א תִתְחַבַּ֔ל

"will not be destroyed"

The expression will not be destroyed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no power can destroy]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 6:27 (#1)
content:
מְשֵׁיזִ֣ב וּ⁠מַצִּ֗ל

"delivering and rescuing"

The terms delivering and rescuing mean similar things. The king is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [powerfully saving people]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 6:27 (#2)
content:
אָתִ֣ין וְ⁠תִמְהִ֔ין

"signs and wonders"

The terms signs and wonders mean similar things. The king is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [amazing miracles]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 6:27 (#3)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁמַיָּ֖⁠א וּ⁠בְ⁠אַרְעָ֑⁠א

"in the heavens and on the earth"

The king is referring to all of creation by naming two major components, the heavens and the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everywhere in creation]

See: Merism

title: Daniel 6:27 (#4)
content:
מִן־יַ֖ד אַרְיָוָתָֽ⁠א

"from the hand of the lions"

Here, hand represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the power of the lions]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel - Chapter 7 Introduction
content:
Daniel 7 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

  1. Narrative introduction: Daniel has a dream about four beasts (1)
  2. Daniel describes his dream (2–15)
  3. Daniel tells how a character in the dream explained its meaning to him (16–27)
  4. Daniel concludes this account personally (28)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 7:9–10 and 7:13–14.

Translation issues in this chapter

Should translations try to identify what the beasts in this dream represent?

The character in the dream who explains its meaning to Daniel tells him, “These great beasts, which are four, are four kings arising from the earth” (7:17). Interpreters have certain understandings of what kingdoms these beasts represent, for example, that the lion represents the Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar, that the bear represents the empire of the Medes and Persians, and so forth. However, we recommend that you do not put anything in the text of your translation or even in a footnote tentatively identifying these kingdoms. Their identity is not certain, and moreover it is not the task of translators to interpret the text, only to represent what it says accurately in their own languages. We recommend similarly that you not offer interpretations of the symbols in chapters 8–12. See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Daniel, “The meaning of Daniel’s visions.”

title: Daniel 7:1 (#1)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת חֲדָ֗ה לְ⁠בֵלְאשַׁצַּר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ בָּבֶ֔ל

"In the year of one to Belshazzar, the king of Babylon"

Daniel is using the time reference In the year of one to Belshazzar, the king of Babylon to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Daniel 7:1 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת חֲדָ֗ה לְ⁠בֵלְאשַׁצַּר֙

"In the year of one to Belshazzar"

In the original language, the number here is a cardinal number, one, that has the sense of an ordinal number, “first.” If your language would not represent a number in a form such as one, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the first year of the reign of Belshazzar]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 7:1 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠בֵלְאשַׁצַּר֙

"to Belshazzar"

The word Belshazzar is the name of a man.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 7:1 (#4)
content:
דָּנִיֵּאל֙ חֵ֣לֶם חֲזָ֔ה וְ⁠חֶזְוֵ֥י רֵאשֵׁ֖⁠הּ עַֽל־מִשְׁכְּבֵ֑⁠הּ בֵּ⁠אדַ֨יִן֙ חֶלְמָ֣⁠א כְתַ֔ב רֵ֥אשׁ מִלִּ֖ין אֲמַֽר

"Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head upon his bed. Then he wrote the dream; he told the head of the matters"

Even though Daniel is the one who is reporting this vision, he is speaking of himself in the third person as Daniel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I saw a dream and visions of my head upon my bed. Then I wrote the dream; I told the head of the matters]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Daniel 7:1 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠חֶזְוֵ֥י רֵאשֵׁ֖⁠הּ

"and visions of his head"

Daniel is using visions of his head as a common expression of the culture to mean “the things that he saw while he was sleeping.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and things that he saw while sleeping]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:1 (#6)
content:
רֵ֥אשׁ מִלִּ֖ין אֲמַֽר

"he told the head of the matters"

Daniel is using the head of the matters as a common expression of the culture to mean “the most important parts of what he had seen.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he recounted the essential points of what he had seen]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:2 (#1)
content:
עָנֵ֤ה דָנִיֵּאל֙ וְ⁠אָמַ֔ר

"Daniel answered and was saying"

Daniel is using the words answered and was saying to introduce a direct quotation of his own report, which continues to the end of this chapter. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Daniel 7:2 (#2)
content:
אַרְבַּע֙ רוּחֵ֣י שְׁמַיָּ֔⁠א

"the four winds of the heavens"

Daniel is referring to all of the directions by naming the four winds of the heavens, that is, the winds that blow from the four points of the compass. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [winds blowing from all directions across the sky]

See: Merism

title: Daniel 7:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אַרְבַּ֤ע חֵיוָן֙ רַבְרְבָ֔ן סָלְקָ֖ן מִן־יַמָּ֑⁠א

"And four great beasts were coming up from the sea"

Here, four great beasts represent four kings and the kingdoms that they rule, as the interpretation later in this chapter explains. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And four great beasts, which represented four kings, were coming up from the sea]

See: Symbolic Language

title: Daniel 7:3 (#2)
content:
שָׁנְיָ֖ן דָּ֥א מִן־דָּֽא

"this being different from this"

Daniel is using this being different from this as a common expression of the culture to mean “each one was different from the others.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each one being unlike the rest]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:4 (#1)
content:
קַדְמָיְתָ֣⁠א כְ⁠אַרְיֵ֔ה וְ⁠גַפִּ֥ין דִּֽי־נְשַׁ֖ר לַ֑⁠הּ חָזֵ֣ה הֲוֵ֡ית עַד֩ דִּי־מְּרִ֨יטוּ גַפַּ֜י⁠הּ וּ⁠נְטִ֣ילַת מִן־אַרְעָ֗⁠א וְ⁠עַל־רַגְלַ֨יִן֙ כֶּ⁠אֱנָ֣שׁ הֳקִימַ֔ת וּ⁠לְבַ֥ב אֱנָ֖שׁ יְהִ֥יב לַֽ⁠הּ

"The first {was} like a lion, but the wings of an eagle {were} to it. I was looking until that its wings were pulled off, and it was raised from the ground, and on two feet it was stood like a man, and the heart of a man was given to it"

These events did not all happen at the same time; they happened one after another. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [The first was like a lion, but it had the wings of an eagle. I kept watching until its wings were torn off. Next, it was lifted up from the ground. After that, it was made to stand on two feet like a man. Finally, it was given the mind of a man]

See: Connect — Sequential Time Relationship

title: Daniel 7:4 (#2)
content:
קַדְמָיְתָ֣⁠א כְ⁠אַרְיֵ֔ה

"The first {was} like a lion"

The point of this comparison is that just as a lion is strong and majestic, so was The first beast that Daniel saw. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The first was as strong and majestic as a lion]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:4 (#3)
content:
מְּרִ֨יטוּ גַפַּ֜י⁠הּ

"its wings were pulled off"

The expression were pulled off is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone pulled off its wings]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:4 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠נְטִ֣ילַת מִן־אַרְעָ֗⁠א וְ⁠עַל־רַגְלַ֨יִן֙ כֶּ⁠אֱנָ֣שׁ הֳקִימַ֔ת

"and it was raised from the ground, and on two feet it was stood like a man"

The expressions was raised and was stood are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and someone raised it from the ground and made it stand on two feet like a man]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:4 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠נְטִ֣ילַת מִן־אַרְעָ֗⁠א וְ⁠עַל־רַגְלַ֨יִן֙ כֶּ⁠אֱנָ֣שׁ הֳקִימַ֔ת

"and it was raised from the ground, and on two feet it was stood like a man"

The point of this comparison is that just as a man stands upright on two feet, so did this beast once its wings were gone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it was raised from the ground, and it was made to stand upright on two feet, in the way that a man stands]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:4 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠עַל־רַגְלַ֨יִן֙

"and on two feet"

The expression two feet is the dual of “feet.” If your language has a dual form, it would be appropriate to use it here.

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 7:4 (#7)
content:
כֶּ⁠אֱנָ֣שׁ

"like a man"

Here the masculine term man has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [like a human being]

See: When Masculine Words Include Women

title: Daniel 7:4 (#8)
content:
וּ⁠לְבַ֥ב אֱנָ֖שׁ יְהִ֥יב לַֽ⁠הּ

"and the heart of a man was given to it"

The expression was given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and someone gave it the heart of a man]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:4 (#9)
content:
וּ⁠לְבַ֥ב אֱנָ֖שׁ יְהִ֥יב לַֽ⁠הּ

"and the heart of a man was given to it"

Here Daniel is speaking as if the ability to think as a human being does were the heart of a man. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it was given the ability to think as a man does]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:5 (#1)
content:
דָּמְיָ֣ה לְ⁠דֹ֗ב

"resembling a bear"

The point of this comparison is that just as a bear is heavy and powerful, so was this second beast. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [resembling a bear, which is heavy and powerful]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׂטַר־חַד֙ הֳקִמַ֔ת

"And on one side, it was raised up"

The expression it was raised up is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And it raised up one of its sides]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:5 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׂטַר־חַד֙ הֳקִמַ֔ת

"And on one side, it was raised up"

The implication is either that the beast reared up on one side as if it were ready to attack or that one of its sides was higher than the other. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And it was rearing up on one side, ready to attack]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:5 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠כֵן֙ אָמְרִ֣ין לַ֔⁠הּ ק֥וּמִֽי אֲכֻ֖לִי בְּשַׂ֥ר שַׂגִּֽיא

"and thus they were saying to it, ‘Arise, devour much flesh"

There is a direct quotation inside a direct quotation here. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and thus they were telling it to arise and devour much flesh]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Daniel 7:5 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠כֵן֙ אָמְרִ֣ין לַ֔⁠הּ

"and thus they were saying to it"

The pronoun they refers to speakers whom Daniel does not identify. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and thus voices were saying to it]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 7:5 (#6)
content:
ק֥וּמִֽי

"Arise"

These speakers are using Arise as a common expression of the culture to mean “Go ahead.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Go ahead]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:6 (#1)
content:
כִּ⁠נְמַ֔ר

"like a leopard"

The point of this comparison is that just as a leopard is swift, so was this beast. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as swift as a leopard]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:6 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁלְטָ֖ן יְהִ֥יב לַֽ⁠הּ

"and dominion was given to it"

The expression was given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God gave dominion to it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁלְטָ֖ן

"and dominion"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of dominion, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the right to rule over others]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 7:7 (#1)
content:
דְּחִילָה֩ וְ⁠אֵֽימְתָנִ֨י

"making afraid and terrible"

The expressions making afraid and terrible mean similar things. Daniel is using the two expressions together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extremely terrifying]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 7:7 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠שְׁאָרָ֖⁠א ב⁠רגלי⁠ה רָפְסָ֑ה

"and it was trampling the rest with its feet"

The implication is that the rest refers either to whatever this beast did not devour or to the other beasts. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and it was trampling with its feet whatever was left over]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:7 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠קַרְנַ֥יִן עֲשַׂ֖ר

"and ten horns"

Here, ten horns represent ten kings, as the interpretation in verse 24 explains. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and ten horns representing ten kings]

See: Symbolic Language

title: Daniel 7:8 (#1)
content:
קֶ֣רֶן אָחֳרִ֤י זְעֵירָה֙ סִלְקָ֣ת ביני⁠הון

"another horn, little, was coming up among them"

Here, another horn, little represents another king who comes to power after those ten kings. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote. Alternate translation: [another horn, little, was coming up among them, which represented another king]

See: Symbolic Language

title: Daniel 7:8 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠תְלָ֗ת מִן־קַרְנַיָּ⁠א֙ קַדְמָ֣יָתָ֔⁠א אתעקרו מִן־קדמי⁠ה

"and three of the first horns were uprooted from before it"

The expression were uprooted is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it pulled out three of the first horns]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:8 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠תְלָ֗ת מִן־קַרְנַיָּ⁠א֙ קַדְמָ֣יָתָ֔⁠א אתעקרו מִן־קדמי⁠ה

"and three of the first horns were uprooted from before it"

Here Daniel is speaking as if three kings losing their power were three horns being uprooted like plants pulled out of the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and three of the first horns were removed from before it]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:8 (#4)
content:
עַיְנִ֜ין כְּ⁠עַיְנֵ֤י אֲנָשָׁ⁠א֙

"eyes like the eyes of a man"

The point of this comparison is that just as the eyes of a man show intelligence and awareness, so did the eyes of this horn. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [eyes that showed intelligence and awareness]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:8 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠פֻ֖ם מְמַלִּ֥ל רַבְרְבָֽן

"and a mouth speaking great {things"

Here, a mouth represents the ability to speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and it was able to speak arrogant words]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 7:8 (#6)
content:
רַבְרְבָֽן

"great {things"

The implication is that the great things that this horn speaks are boastful claims that it makes about itself. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [arrogant boasts about itself]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:9 (#1)
content:
כָרְסָוָן֙ רְמִ֔יו

"thrones were set"

The expression were set is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone set up thrones]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:9 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עַתִּ֥יק יוֹמִ֖ין

"and the Ancient of Days"

Daniel is using the Ancient of Days as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who has always existed,” that is, God. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the eternal God]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:9 (#3)
content:
לְבוּשֵׁ֣⁠הּ ׀ כִּ⁠תְלַ֣ג חִוָּ֗ר

"His clothing {was} white as snow"

The point of this comparison is that just as snow is bright white, so was His clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [His clothing was gleaming, bright white]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:9 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠שְׂעַ֤ר רֵאשֵׁ⁠הּ֙ כַּ⁠עֲמַ֣ר נְקֵ֔א

"and the hair of his head {was} like pure wool"

The point of this comparison is that just as pure wool is white, so was the hair of his head. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the hair of his head was white, like pure wool]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:9 (#5)
content:
כָּרְסְיֵ⁠הּ֙ שְׁבִיבִ֣ין דִּי־נ֔וּר

"His throne {was} flames of fire"

Here Daniel is speaking as if this throne were flames of fire. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His throne appeared to be on fire]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:9 (#6)
content:
נ֔וּר גַּלְגִּלּ֖וֹ⁠הִי נ֥וּר דָּלִֽק

"fire; its wheels {were} burning fire"

The implication is that the mention of its wheels pictures this throne as a chariot. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [fire; it was like a chariot, and its wheels were burning fire]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:10 (#1)
content:
נְהַ֣ר דִּי־נ֗וּר נָגֵ֤ד וְ⁠נָפֵק֙ מִן־קֳדָמ֔וֹ⁠הִי

"A river of fire was flowing and coming out from before him"

Here Daniel is speaking as if the fire coming out from God’s presence were a stream of water that was flowing like a river. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Fire was continuously coming out from before him in great quantity]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:10 (#2)
content:
אֶ֤לֶף אלפים יְשַׁמְּשׁוּנֵּ֔⁠הּ וְ⁠רִבּ֥וֹ רבון קָֽדָמ֣וֹ⁠הִי יְקוּמ֑וּן

"a thousand of thousands served him, and a myriad of myriads stood before him"

The expressions a thousand of thousands and a myriad of myriads indicate very large numbers of beings. Translate these numbers according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [a million served him, and a hundred million stood before him]

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 7:10 (#3)
content:
אֶ֤לֶף אלפים יְשַׁמְּשׁוּנֵּ֔⁠הּ וְ⁠רִבּ֥וֹ רבון קָֽדָמ֣וֹ⁠הִי יְקוּמ֑וּן

"a thousand of thousands served him, and a myriad of myriads stood before him"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [an extremely large number of people served him and stood before him]

See: Parallelism

title: Daniel 7:10 (#4)
content:
קָֽדָמ֣וֹ⁠הִי יְקוּמ֑וּן

"stood before him"

Here Daniel is speaking as if being ready to serve someone were to have stood before him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [waited in his presence, ready to serve him]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:10 (#5)
content:
דִּינָ֥⁠א יְתִ֖ב

"The court sat"

Here Daniel is speaking as if beginning a session of judgment were simply to have sat down. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The court convened to render judgment]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:10 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠סִפְרִ֥ין פְּתִֽיחוּ

"and books were opened"

The expression were opened is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the attendants opened the books]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:10 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠סִפְרִ֥ין פְּתִֽיחוּ

"and books were opened"

The implication is that these books contain the records of what people have done, which the court uses in judging them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they opened the records of everything people had done, in order to judge them by those records]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:11 (#1)
content:
מִן

"from"

The word translated as from indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because of]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Daniel 7:11 (#2)
content:
קְטִילַ֤ת חֵֽיוְתָ⁠א֙ וְ⁠הוּבַ֣ד גִּשְׁמַ֔⁠הּ וִ⁠יהִיבַ֖ת לִ⁠יקֵדַ֥ת אֶשָּֽׁא

"the beast was killed and its body was destroyed and it was given to the burning fire"

The expressions was killed, was destroyed, and was given are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God killed the beast and destroyed its body and put it into the burning fire]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:12 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠שְׁאָר֙ חֵֽיוָתָ֔⁠א הֶעְדִּ֖יו שָׁלְטָנְ⁠ה֑וֹן

"And the rest of the beasts, they took away their dominion"

Daniel mentions the rest of the beasts first and then says what was done to them. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what was done to these beasts together with the mention of the beasts themselves. Alternate translation: [And they took away the dominion of the rest of the beasts]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 7:12 (#2)
content:
הֶעְדִּ֖יו שָׁלְטָנְ⁠ה֑וֹן

"they took away their dominion"

The pronoun they refers to beings whom Daniel does not identify, not to the beasts. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they lost their dominion to certain beings whom Daniel does not name]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 7:12 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אַרְכָ֧ה בְ⁠חַיִּ֛ין יְהִ֥יבַת לְ⁠ה֖וֹן עַד־זְמַ֥ן וְ⁠עִדָּֽן

"but a prolonging in life was given to them for a season and a time"

The expression was given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but God prolonged their lives for a season and a time]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:12 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אַרְכָ֧ה בְ⁠חַיִּ֛ין

"but a prolonging in life"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of a prolonging, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but a longer time to live]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 7:12 (#5)
content:
עַד־זְמַ֥ן וְ⁠עִדָּֽן

"for a season and a time"

Daniel is using for a season and a time as a common expression of the culture to mean “for a limited period of time that he does not specify.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for a certain period of time]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:13 (#1)
content:
עִם־עֲנָנֵ֣י שְׁמַיָּ֔⁠א

"with the clouds of the heavens"

Here, the clouds of the heavens represent coming from heaven, where God dwells. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from God’s dwelling place in heaven]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 7:13 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠בַ֥ר אֱנָ֖שׁ אָתֵ֣ה הֲוָ֑ה

"one like a son of man was coming"

The point of this comparison is that just as a son of man has a human form, so did this one whom Daniel saw. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [one who had a human form was coming]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 7:13 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠קְדָמ֖וֹ⁠הִי הַקְרְבֽוּ⁠הִי

"and they brought him near before him"

The pronoun they refers to attendants whom Daniel does not identify, the first him refers to the one like a son of man, and the second him refers to the Ancient of Days. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and attendants brought him near before the Ancient of Days]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 7:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֵ֨⁠הּ יְהִ֤יב שָׁלְטָן֙ וִ⁠יקָ֣ר וּ⁠מַלְכ֔וּ וְ⁠כֹ֣ל עַֽמְמַיָּ֗⁠א אֻמַיָּ֛⁠א וְ⁠לִשָּׁנַיָּ֖⁠א לֵ֣⁠הּ יִפְלְח֑וּן שָׁלְטָנֵ֞⁠הּ שָׁלְטָ֤ן עָלַם֙ דִּֽי־לָ֣א יֶעְדֵּ֔ה וּ⁠מַלְכוּתֵ֖⁠הּ דִּי־לָ֥א תִתְחַבַּֽל

"And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion {is} a dominion of eternity that will not pass away, and his kingdom {is one} that will not be destroyed"

Here, that marks all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him as the goal or purpose of giving him dominion and glory and a kingdom. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Daniel 7:14 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֵ֨⁠הּ יְהִ֤יב שָׁלְטָן֙ וִ⁠יקָ֣ר וּ⁠מַלְכ֔וּ

"And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom"

The expression was given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Ancient of Days gave him dominion and glory and a kingdom]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:14 (#3)
content:
שָׁלְטָן֙ וִ⁠יקָ֣ר וּ⁠מַלְכ֔וּ

"dominion and glory and a kingdom"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of dominion, glory, and a kingdom, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [the ability to rule and to be honored and to reign as king]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 7:14 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠כֹ֣ל עַֽמְמַיָּ֗⁠א אֻמַיָּ֛⁠א וְ⁠לִשָּׁנַיָּ֖⁠א

"that all peoples, nations, and languages"

The terms peoples, nations, and languages mean similar things. Daniel is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [that everyone in the whole world]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 7:14 (#5)
content:
שָׁלְטָנֵ֞⁠הּ שָׁלְטָ֤ן עָלַם֙ דִּֽי־לָ֣א יֶעְדֵּ֔ה וּ⁠מַלְכוּתֵ֖⁠הּ דִּי־לָ֥א תִתְחַבַּֽל

"His dominion {is} a dominion of eternity that will not pass away, and his kingdom {is one} that will not be destroyed"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [His royal rule will certainly endure forever]

See: Parallelism

title: Daniel 7:14 (#6)
content:
שָׁלְטָ֤ן עָלַם֙

"is} a dominion of eternity"

Daniel is using the possessive form to describe a dominion that is characterized by eternity. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a dominion that lasts forever]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 7:14 (#7)
content:
דִּי־לָ֥א תִתְחַבַּֽל

"is one} that will not be destroyed"

The expression will not be destroyed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is one that nothing will ever destroy]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:15 (#1)
content:
אֶתְכְּרִיַּ֥ת רוּחִ֛⁠י אֲנָ֥ה דָנִיֵּ֖אל בְּ⁠ג֣וֹא נִדְנֶ֑ה

"My spirit was distressed, I, Daniel, in the midst of the body"

Daniel interrupts his statement about his spirit in order to identify himself. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about I, Daniel before the information about his spirit being distressed. Alternate translation: [As for me, Daniel, my spirit within my body was distressed]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 7:15 (#2)
content:
אֶתְכְּרִיַּ֥ת רוּחִ֛⁠י אֲנָ֥ה דָנִיֵּ֖אל בְּ⁠ג֣וֹא נִדְנֶ֑ה

"My spirit was distressed, I, Daniel, in the midst of the body"

Daniel is using My spirit was distressed as a common expression of the culture to mean “I was deeply troubled within myself.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I, Daniel, was deeply troubled]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:16 (#1)
content:
חַד֙ מִן־קָ֣אֲמַיָּ֔⁠א

"one of the ones standing"

Here Daniel is introducing one of the ones standing as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain man who was standing there]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Daniel 7:16 (#2)
content:
חַד֙ מִן־קָ֣אֲמַיָּ֔⁠א

"one of the ones standing"

The implication is that this is one of the many beings who were standing before God, as verse 10 describes. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [one of the ones standing before God]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:16 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠פְשַׁ֥ר מִלַּיָּ֖⁠א יְהוֹדְעִנַּֽ⁠נִי

"and he made me know the interpretation of the matters"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the interpretation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he made me know what the matters meant]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 7:17 (#1)
content:
אִלֵּין֙ חֵיוָתָ֣⁠א רַבְרְבָתָ֔⁠א

"These great beasts"

This is the beginning of what the one of the ones standing told Daniel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could introduce this as a direct quotation of him. Alternate translation: [He told me, ‘These great beasts]

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Daniel 7:17 (#2)
content:
אִלֵּין֙ חֵיוָתָ֣⁠א רַבְרְבָתָ֔⁠א דִּ֥י אִנִּ֖ין אַרְבַּ֑ע אַרְבְּעָ֥ה מַלְכִ֖ין יְקוּמ֥וּן מִן־אַרְעָֽ⁠א

"These great beasts, which are four, {are} four kings arising from the earth"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [He told me that those great beasts, which were four, were four kings arising from the earth]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Daniel 7:17 (#3)
content:
אַרְבְּעָ֥ה מַלְכִ֖ין יְקוּמ֥וּן מִן־אַרְעָֽ⁠א

"are} four kings arising from the earth"

Here, four kings represent the four kingdoms that these kings rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [are four kingdoms that will arise on the earth]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 7:17 (#4)
content:
יְקוּמ֥וּן מִן־אַרְעָֽ⁠א

"arising from the earth"

The attendant is using arising from the earth as a common expression of the culture to mean “coming to power in the world.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who will come to power in the world]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:18 (#1)
content:
וִֽ⁠יקַבְּלוּן֙

"But & will receive"

The attendant uses the word But here to indicate a contrast between the four kings who arise from the earth and the holy people of God who receive the kingdom. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However,]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Daniel 7:18 (#2)
content:
וִֽ⁠יקַבְּלוּן֙ מַלְכוּתָ֔⁠א קַדִּישֵׁ֖י עֶלְיוֹנִ֑ין

"But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the kingdom, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But the saints of the Most High will start to reign]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 7:18 (#3)
content:
קַדִּישֵׁ֖י עֶלְיוֹנִ֑ין

"the saints of the Most High"

The attendant is using the possessive form to describe the saints who belong to the Most High. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the holy people who belong to the Most High]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 7:18 (#4)
content:
קַדִּישֵׁ֖י עֶלְיוֹנִ֑ין

"the saints of the Most High"

The implication is that the saints are the people whom God has set apart as holy for himself. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the people whom God has set apart as holy for himself]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:18 (#5)
content:
עַֽד־עָ֣לְמָ֔⁠א וְ⁠עַ֖ד עָלַ֥ם עָלְמַיָּֽ⁠א

"to eternity and to eternity of eternities"

The expressions to eternity and to eternity of eternities mean similar things. The attendant is using the two expressions together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [forever without end]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 7:19 (#1)
content:
דִּֽי־הֲוָ֥ת שָֽׁנְיָ֖ה מִן־כל⁠הון דְּחִילָ֣ה יַתִּ֗ירָה שני⁠ה דִּֽי־פַרְזֶל֙ וְ⁠טִפְרַ֣י⁠הּ דִּֽי־נְחָ֔שׁ אָֽכְלָ֣ה מַדֲּקָ֔ה וּ⁠שְׁאָרָ֖⁠א בְּ⁠רַגְלַ֥י⁠הּ רָֽפְסָֽה

"which was being different from all of them, making afraid exceedingly, its teeth of iron and its claws of bronze, devouring, crushing, and trampling the rest with its feet"

Daniel gives a long series of descriptions of the fourth beast within one sentence. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what this beast looked like and what it did into separate sentences. Alternate translation: [which was different from all of them. It was exceedingly frightening. Its teeth were iron and its claws were bronze. It devoured and crushed, and it trampled the rest with its feet]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 7:20 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠פֻם֙ מְמַלִּ֣ל רַבְרְבָ֔ן

"and a mouth speaking great {things"

Daniel is using speaking great things as a common expression of the culture to mean “boasting arrogantly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a mouth that boasted proudly] or [a mouth that spoke arrogant words]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:20 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠חֶזְוַ֖⁠הּ רַ֥ב מִן־חַבְרָתַֽ⁠הּ

"and its appearance {was} greater than its fellows"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of its appearance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and it looked more imposing than its fellows]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 7:22 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠דִינָ֣⁠א יְהִ֔ב לְ⁠קַדִּישֵׁ֖י עֶלְיוֹנִ֑ין

"and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High"

The expression was given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he gave judgment for the saints of the Most High]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:22 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠דִינָ֣⁠א יְהִ֔ב לְ⁠קַדִּישֵׁ֖י עֶלְיוֹנִ֑ין

"and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High"

The implication is either that the court ruled in favor of God’s holy people or that the authority to judge was given to God’s holy people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the court ruled in favor of the saints of the Most High]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:23 (#1)
content:
כֵּן֮ אֲמַר֒ חֵֽיוְתָ⁠א֙ רְבִיעָ֣יְתָ֔⁠א מַלְכ֤וּ רביעי⁠א תֶּהֱוֵ֣א בְ⁠אַרְעָ֔⁠א

"Thus he was saying, ‘The fourth beast will be a fourth kingdom on the earth"

There is a direct quotation inside a direct quotation here. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Thus he was saying that the fourth beast will be a fourth kingdom on the earth]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Daniel 7:23 (#2)
content:
כֵּן֮ אֲמַר֒

"Thus he was saying"

The pronoun he refers to the one standing whom Daniel approached, as verse 16 describes. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Thus the one standing there was saying]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 7:23 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠תֵאכֻל֙ כָּל־אַרְעָ֔⁠א וּ⁠תְדוּשִׁנַּ֖⁠הּ וְ⁠תַדְּקִנַּֽ⁠הּ

"And it will devour all of the earth, and it will trample it and crush it"

Here the attendant is speaking as if this kingdom were a beast that would devour the nations it conquered and trample and crush them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will conquer all of the earth, and it will defeat and destroy every nation]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:23 (#4)
content:
כָּל־אַרְעָ֔⁠א

"all of the earth"

The attendant says all of the earth as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [a vast expanse of land]

See: Hyperbole

title: Daniel 7:24 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠קַרְנַיָּ֣⁠א עֲשַׂ֔ר מִנַּ⁠הּ֙ מַלְכוּתָ֔⁠ה עַשְׂרָ֥ה מַלְכִ֖ין יְקֻמ֑וּן

"And the ten horns, from this kingdom, ten kings will arise"

The attendant mentions the ten horns first and then explains in a new clause what they represent. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the ten kings together with the mention of the ten horns. Alternate translation: [And from this kingdom, ten kings, who are the ten horns, will arise]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 7:24 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠ה֤וּא יִשְׁנֵא֙ מִן־קַדְמָיֵ֔⁠א

"And he will be different from the first {ones"

The attendant is using the adjective first as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And he will be different from the kings who ruled before him]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 7:25 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִלִּ֗ין לְ⁠צַ֤ד עלי⁠א יְמַלִּ֔ל

"And he will speak words against the Most High"

The implication is that these words against the Most High are defiant and insulting. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And he will speak arrogant insults against the Most High]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:25 (#2)
content:
עלי⁠א

"the Most High"

The first instance of the Most High is singular, while the second instance is plural. This is an Aramaic plural of excellence. It does not mean that there is more than one God, but that the one true God is supremely glorious and powerful. If your language can use its plural form for intensification, not just for number, it would be appropriate to use it here. Other languages may have other ways to show this intensification. Alternate translation: [the Most High … the Almighty God]

See: Unusual Uses of the Plural

title: Daniel 7:25 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠קַדִּישֵׁ֥י עֶלְיוֹנִ֖ין יְבַלֵּ֑א

"and he will wear out the saints of the Most High"

Here the attendant is speaking as if oppressing God’s holy people relentlessly were to wear out a garment until it fell apart. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will continually afflict the holy people of the Most High until they are exhausted]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 7:25 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠הַשְׁנָיָה֙ זִמְנִ֣ין וְ⁠דָ֔ת

"to change the times and the law"

The implication is that the times are the festivals that God appointed for his people and that the law is the law that God gave them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to change the appointed festivals and the law that God gave his people]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:25 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְיַהֲב֣וּן בִּ⁠ידֵ֔⁠הּ

"And they will be given into his hand"

The expression will be given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And God will put the times and the law into his hand]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:25 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְיַהֲב֣וּן בִּ⁠ידֵ֔⁠הּ

"And they will be given into his hand"

The pronoun they refers to the saints of the Most High, not to the times and the law. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the saints will be given]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 7:25 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְיַהֲב֣וּן בִּ⁠ידֵ֔⁠הּ

"And they will be given into his hand"

Here, his hand represents the power and control of this king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And they will be given over to his power]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 7:25 (#8)
content:
עַד־עִדָּ֥ן וְ⁠עִדָּנִ֖ין וּ⁠פְלַ֥ג עִדָּֽן

"for a time and times and half of a time"

The attendant is using a time and times and half of a time as a common expression of the culture to mean “a limited period that God has determined.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for a limited period that God has determined]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:26 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠הַשְׁמָדָ֥ה וּ⁠לְ⁠הוֹבָדָ֖ה עַד־סוֹפָֽ⁠א

"to consume and destroy {it} to the end"

Here, to marks consume and destroy as the goal or purpose of taking away his dominion. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [totally consuming and destroying it]

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Daniel 7:26 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠הַשְׁמָדָ֥ה וּ⁠לְ⁠הוֹבָדָ֖ה

"to consume and destroy {it"

The terms consume and destroy mean similar things. The attendant is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to utterly destroy it]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 7:26 (#3)
content:
עַד־סוֹפָֽ⁠א

"to the end"

The attendant is using to the end as a common expression of the culture to mean “completely and finally.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [completely and finally]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:27 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מַלְכוּתָ֨⁠ה וְ⁠שָׁלְטָנָ֜⁠א וּ⁠רְבוּתָ֗⁠א דִּ֚י מַלְכְוָת֙

"and the kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of the kingdom, the dominion, and the greatness, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [and the right to reign and to rule gloriously over the kingdoms]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 7:27 (#2)
content:
תְּח֣וֹת כָּל־שְׁמַיָּ֔⁠א

"under all of the heavens"

The attendant says under all of the heavens as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [throughout the entire earth]

See: Hyperbole

title: Daniel 7:27 (#3)
content:
יְהִיבַ֕ת לְ⁠עַ֖ם קַדִּישֵׁ֣י עֶלְיוֹנִ֑ין

"will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High"

The expression will be given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will give to his people, the saints of the Most High]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 7:27 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠כֹל֙ שָׁלְטָ֣נַיָּ֔⁠א לֵ֥⁠הּ יִפְלְח֖וּן וְ⁠יִֽשְׁתַּמְּעֽוּן

"and all dominions will serve and make themselves hear him"

Here, all dominions represent the rulers who hold that authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and all rulers will serve and make themselves hear him]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 7:27 (#5)
content:
לֵ֥⁠הּ יִפְלְח֖וּן וְ⁠יִֽשְׁתַּמְּעֽוּן

"will serve and make themselves hear him"

In this context, the term hear has the sense of “obey.” While the form is reflexive in the original, in many languages an active form will convey the meaning accurately. Alternate translation: [will serve and obey him]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 7:27 (#6)
content:
לֵ֥⁠הּ יִפְלְח֖וּן וְ⁠יִֽשְׁתַּמְּעֽוּן

"will serve and make themselves hear him"

The terms serve and make themselves hear him mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [will diligently obey him] or [will obey him completely]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 7:28 (#1)
content:
עַד־כָּ֖ה סוֹפָ֣⁠א דִֽי־מִלְּתָ֑⁠א

"To here {is} the end of the matter"

The words To here signal the end of Daniel’s report of what he saw in his vision. Use the natural form in your language for expressing the conclusion of an account. Alternate translation: [That is the end of my report]

See: End of Story

title: Daniel 7:28 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠זִיוַ⁠י֙ יִשְׁתַּנּ֣וֹן עֲלַ֔⁠י

"and my splendors changed upon me"

Daniel is using my splendors changed upon me as a common expression of the culture to mean “my face turned pale.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my face turned pale]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 7:28 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מִלְּתָ֖⁠א בְּ⁠לִבִּ֥⁠י נִטְרֵֽת

"But I kept the matter in my heart"

Here Daniel is speaking as if his heart were a container in which he could keep something. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But I did not tell anyone what I had seen]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel - Chapter 8 Introduction
content:
Daniel 8 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

  1. Daniel sees a vision of a ram, a goat, and a horn that became great (1–14)
  2. The angel Gabriel explains the vision to Daniel (15–27)

Translation issues in this chapter

The meaning of the animals in this vision

In the case of this vision, the interpretation that a figure gives to Daniel does specify what the animals represent. Gabriel tells Daniel, “The ram that you saw … is the kings of Media and Persia” (8:20) and “The male goat is the king of Javan” (that is, Greece, 8:21). There is no reason not to include this specific information in your translation. However, the identity of the king in verses 23–25 is not certain, and we recommend that you not suggest in your translation who this might be.

title: Daniel 8:1 (#1)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת שָׁל֔וֹשׁ לְ⁠מַלְכ֖וּת

"In the year of three to the reign of"

The expression In the year of three uses a number in a form that means the third year of Belshazzar’s reign. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as this, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the third year of the reign of]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 8:1 (#2)
content:
בֵּלְאשַׁצַּ֣ר הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ

"King Belshazzar"

The word Belshazzar is the name of a man.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 8:1 (#3)
content:
חָז֞וֹן נִרְאָ֤ה אֵלַ⁠י֙ אֲנִ֣י דָנִיֵּ֔אל

"a vision appeared to me, me, Daniel"

Daniel is stating the pronoun me separately, even though the expression to me already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that the vision he is describing is one that he saw personally. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [to me, Daniel, personally]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 8:1 (#4)
content:
אֵלַ⁠י֙ אֲנִ֣י דָנִיֵּ֔אל

"to me, me, Daniel"

Daniel is repeating forms of the word me in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [to me indeed, Daniel]

See: Reduplication

title: Daniel 8:1 (#5)
content:
אַחֲרֵ֛י הַ⁠נִּרְאָ֥ה אֵלַ֖⁠י בַּ⁠תְּחִלָּֽה

"after the one having appeared to me at the first"

The implication is that the one having appeared to me at the first refers to the vision that Daniel describes in the previous chapter. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [after the earlier vision that had appeared to me, the one I have just described]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:2 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠שׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַ⁠בִּירָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּ⁠עֵילָ֣ם הַ⁠מְּדִינָ֑ה

"was} in Susa the citadel, which {is} in Elam the province"

The word Susa is the name of a city, and the word Elam is the name of a province. Later in this verse, Ulai is the name of a canal.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 8:3 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֤א עֵינַ⁠י֙

"And I lifted up my eyes"

Daniel is using I lifted up my eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “I looked up.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I looked up]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֣ה

"and behold"

Daniel is using the word behold as if he wanted his readers to look at something, when he actually wants them to pay attention to what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and hear this]

See: Foreground Information

title: Daniel 8:3 (#3)
content:
עֹמֵ֛ד לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י הָ⁠אֻבָ֖ל

"standing to the face of the canal"

Here, the face of the canal represents “the area in front of the canal.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [standing in front of the canal]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 8:3 (#4)
content:
קְרָנָ֑יִם וְ⁠הַ⁠קְּרָנַ֣יִם

"were} two horns, and the two horns"

In each instance, the expression two horns is the dual of “horn.” If your language has a dual form, it would be appropriate to use it here.

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 8:3 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אַחַת֙ גְּבֹהָ֣ה מִן־הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֔ית וְ⁠הַ֨⁠גְּבֹהָ֔ה עֹלָ֖ה בָּ⁠אַחֲרֹנָֽה

"but the one was higher than the second, and the higher came up afterward"

Daniel is using the adjectives the one, the second, and the higher as nouns to mean certain horns. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [but one horn was higher than the other horn, and the higher horn came up afterward]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 8:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠כָל־חַיּוֹת֙ לֹֽא־יַֽעַמְד֣וּ לְ⁠פָנָ֔י⁠ו

"and all of the beasts did not stand to its face"

Daniel is using did not stand to its face as a common expression of the culture to mean “could not withstand it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and no beast could withstand it]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:4 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֥ין מַצִּ֖יל מִ⁠יָּד֑⁠וֹ

"and there was none delivering from its hand"

Here, its hand represents “its power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and there was none delivering from its power]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 8:4 (#3)
content:
כִ⁠רְצֹנ֖⁠וֹ

"according to its will"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of will, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as it wanted]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 8:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֣י ׀ הָיִ֣יתִי מֵבִ֗ין

"And I, I was observing"

Daniel is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I was observing already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he was carefully watching this vision as it unfolded. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I was watching closely]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 8:5 (#2)
content:
עַל־פְּנֵ֣י כָל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ

"over the face of all of the earth"

Daniel is using the face of all of the earth as a common expression of the culture to mean “the whole surface of the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [over the entire surface of the earth]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:5 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֥ין נוֹגֵ֖עַ בָּ⁠אָ֑רֶץ

"but without touching the earth"

The implication is that the goat was moving so swiftly that it seemed not to touch the ground as it ran. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [but moving so swiftly that it seemed not to touch the earth]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:5 (#4)
content:
קֶ֥רֶן חָז֖וּת

"a horn of vision"

Daniel is using a horn of vision as a common expression of the culture to mean “a conspicuous horn.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a prominent horn]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:6 (#1)
content:
בַּ֣עַל הַ⁠קְּרָנַ֔יִם

"the master of two horns"

Daniel is using the master of two horns as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one that had two horns.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one that had the two horns]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:6 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠קְּרָנַ֔יִם

"two horns"

As in verse 3, the expression two horns is the dual of “horn.” See how you translated that expression there.

title: Daniel 8:6 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֻבָ֑ל

"to the face of the canal"

Here, to the face of represents being in front of the canal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [beside] or [in front of]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 8:6 (#4)
content:
בַּ⁠חֲמַ֥ת כֹּחֽ⁠וֹ

"in the heat of its power"

Daniel is using in the heat of its power as a common expression of the culture to mean “with furious strength.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with furious strength]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:7 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּתְמַרְמַ֤ר אֵלָי⁠ו֙

"and it was embittered at it"

Daniel is speaking as if the goat was embittered in order to describe how enraged it was at the ram. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the goat was enraged at the ram]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 8:7 (#2)
content:
אֶת־שְׁתֵּ֣י קְרָנָ֔י⁠ו

"the two of its horns"

In this instance, the term horns is plural, not dual as in verses 3 and 6. Translate this in the way your language would naturally express numbers.

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 8:7 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠יָּדֽ⁠וֹ

"from its hand"

Here, hand represents the power/control of the goat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the goat’s power]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 8:7 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־הָ֥יָה כֹ֛חַ בָּ⁠אַ֖יִל לַ⁠עֲמֹ֣ד לְ⁠פָנָ֑י⁠ו

"And the ram was not strong to stand to its face"

Daniel is using stand to its face as a common expression of the culture to mean “resist it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was not strong enough to resist the goat] or [could not withstand the goat]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:7 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠יַּשְׁלִיכֵ֤⁠הוּ אַ֨רְצָ⁠ה֙ וַֽ⁠יִּרְמְסֵ֔⁠הוּ

"And it cast it to the earth and trampled it"

The first pronoun it in this sentence refers to the goat, and the pronouns that follow refer to the ram. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the goat cast the ram to the earth and trampled it]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 8:8 (#1)
content:
נִשְׁבְּרָה֙ הַ⁠קֶּ֣רֶן הַ⁠גְּדוֹלָ֔ה

"the great horn was broken"

The expression was broken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [something broke off the great horn]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 8:8 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠אַרְבַּ֖ע רוּח֥וֹת הַ⁠שָּׁמָֽיִם

"toward the four winds of the heavens"

Daniel is speaking as if the four directions were the four winds of the heavens. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [toward the four directions of the earth]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 8:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֶל־הַ⁠צֶּֽבִי

"and toward the Beauty"

Here, the Beauty represents “the land of Israel.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and toward the glorious land of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 8:10 (#1)
content:
צְבָ֣א הַ⁠שָּׁמָ֑יִם

"the army of the heavens"
