Daniel is speaking of the beings who live in heaven as if they were the army of the heavens. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the heavenly beings]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 8:11 (#1)
content:
שַֽׂר־הַ⁠צָּבָ֖א

"the commander of the army"

The implication is that the commander of the army is God, who rules over the beings who live in heaven. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God, who commands the army of heaven]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:11 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מִמֶּ֨⁠נּוּ֙ הרים הַ⁠תָּמִ֔יד וְ⁠הֻשְׁלַ֖ךְ מְכ֥וֹן מִקְדָּשֽׁ⁠וֹ

"And the perpetual sacrifice was removed from him, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down"

The expressions was removed and was cast down are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And it took away the perpetual sacrifice from him, and it threw down the place of his sanctuary]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 8:11 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠תָּמִ֔יד

"the perpetual sacrifice"

The implication is that the perpetual sacrifice is the offering that the priests presented to God every morning and every evening. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the sacrifice that the priests offered to God every morning and evening]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:12 (#1)
content:
תִּנָּתֵ֥ן

"will be given over"

The expression will be given over is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God will hand an army over]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 8:12 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠תַשְׁלֵ֤ךְ אֱמֶת֙ אַ֔רְצָ⁠ה

"and it will cast truth to the ground"

Daniel is speaking as if truth were an object that could be thrown down when he says that the horn will cast truth to the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it will utterly reject the truth]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 8:12 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עָשְׂתָ֖ה וְ⁠הִצְלִֽיחָה

"And it will do and succeed"

The phrase do and succeed expresses a single idea. The word succeed tells more about do. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And it will do whatever it wishes with success]

See: Hendiadys

title: Daniel 8:13 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשְׁמְעָ֥⁠ה אֶֽחָד־קָד֖וֹשׁ מְדַבֵּ֑ר

"And I heard a holy one speaking"

The implication is that a holy one is an angel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And I heard a holy angel speaking]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:13 (#2)
content:
תֵּ֛ת וְ⁠קֹ֥דֶשׁ וְ⁠צָבָ֖א מִרְמָֽס

"the giving {of} both the sanctuary and the army for trampling"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the giving, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that God will give over for trampling both the sanctuary and the army]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 8:13 (#3)
content:
מִרְמָֽס

"for trampling"

The holy one is speaking of the defeat and desecration of the sanctuary and the army as if enemies would crush them underfoot, since they have been given for trampling. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to be crushed by enemies]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 8:14 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלַ֔⁠י

"And he said to me"

The pronoun he refers to the holy one who was speaking, whom Daniel mentioned first in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And that first holy one said to me]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 8:14 (#2)
content:
אֵלַ֔⁠י

"to me"

Some ancient manuscripts read “to me.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “to him.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

title: Daniel 8:14 (#3)
content:
עַ֚ד עֶ֣רֶב בֹּ֔קֶר אַלְפַּ֖יִם וּ⁠שְׁלֹ֣שׁ מֵא֑וֹת

"Until evening, morning, 2,300"

The number 2,300 counts pairs of an evening and a morning, that is, the times when the priests presented the perpetual sacrifice. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Until 2,300 evenings and mornings have passed]

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 8:14 (#4)
content:
עַ֚ד עֶ֣רֶב בֹּ֔קֶר

"Until evening, morning"

The holy one is referring to all of each day by naming two major components, evening and morning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Until there have passed full days numbering]

See: Merism

title: Daniel 8:14 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠נִצְדַּ֖ק קֹֽדֶשׁ

"Then the sanctuary will be made right"

The expression will be made right is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then God will make the sanctuary right]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 8:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֛ה

"And behold"

Daniel is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And listen]

See: Foreground Information

title: Daniel 8:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֛ה עֹמֵ֥ד לְ⁠נֶגְדִּ֖⁠י

"And behold, one standing to my face"

Daniel is introducing one standing to my face as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And suddenly there was someone standing in front of me]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Daniel 8:15 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֛ה עֹמֵ֥ד לְ⁠נֶגְדִּ֖⁠י

"And behold, one standing to my face"

Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. It may be helpful to supply these words from the context. Alternate translation: [behold, I saw one standing in front of me]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 8:15 (#4)
content:
כְּ⁠מַרְאֵה־גָֽבֶר

"according to the appearance of a man"

Daniel says that this being was according to the appearance of a man. The point of this comparison is that the one standing before him looked like a human being, although he was not actually a man. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [who looked like a human being, although he was not one]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 8:16 (#1)
content:
בֵּ֣ין אוּלָ֑י

"between the Ulai"

Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [coming from between the banks of the Ulai]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 8:16 (#2)
content:
הָבֵ֥ן לְ⁠הַלָּ֖ז אֶת־הַ⁠מַּרְאֶֽה

"make this one understand the appearance"

The pronoun this one refers to Daniel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [make Daniel understand the appearance]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 8:17 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּבֹא֙ אֵ֣צֶל עָמְדִ֔⁠י

"And he came beside my standing"

Daniel is using beside my standing as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the place where I was standing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he came to the place where I was standing]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:17 (#2)
content:
וָ⁠אֶפְּלָ֖⁠ה עַל־פָּנָ֑⁠י

"and fell on my face"

Falling face down on the ground was a symbolic action by which Daniel showed fear and reverence in the presence of this heavenly messenger. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and fell down with my face to the ground to show reverence]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Daniel 8:17 (#3)
content:
בֶּן־אָדָ֔ם

"son of man"

Gabriel is using son of man as a common expression of the culture to mean “mortal human being.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human being]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:19 (#1)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִ֣י מוֹדִֽיעֲ⁠ךָ֔

"Behold me, making you know"

Gabriel is using Behold me, making you know as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to make you know.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to tell you]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:19 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠אַחֲרִ֣ית הַ⁠זָּ֑עַם

"at the end of the indignation"

The implication is that the indignation is God’s anger against sinful people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the end of God’s anger against sinners]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:20 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠אַ֥יִל אֲשֶׁר־רָאִ֖יתָ בַּ֣עַל הַ⁠קְּרָנָ֑יִם מַלְכֵ֖י מָדַ֥י וּ⁠פָרָֽס

"The ram that you saw, a master of two horns, {is} the kings of Media and Persia"

Gabriel is speaking as if The ram that Daniel saw were the same thing as the kings of Media and Persia, when he means that the ram represents them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The ram that you saw, a master of two horns, represents the kings of Media and Persia]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 8:21 (#1)
content:
יָוָ֑ן

"Javan"

The word Javan is the name of a people group. The home of those people is known in many languages today as “Greece.” You could use that name in your translation if this would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Greece]

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 8:21 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠קֶּ֤רֶן הַ⁠גְּדוֹלָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בֵּין־עֵינָ֔י⁠ו ה֖וּא הַ⁠מֶּ֥לֶךְ הָ⁠רִאשֽׁוֹן

"and the great horn that {was} between its eyes, it {is} the first king"

Gabriel names the great horn first and then refers back to it with the pronoun it. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the horn and the information about the king together in a single statement. Alternate translation: [and the great horn that was between its eyes represents the first king]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 8:22 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א בְ⁠כֹחֽ⁠וֹ

"but not with its power"

Gabriel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but they will not stand with the power it has]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 8:23 (#1)
content:
וּֽ⁠בְ⁠אַחֲרִית֙ מַלְכוּתָ֔⁠ם

"And at the end of their rule"

The pronoun their refers to the four kingdoms that Gabriel described in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And at the end of these kingdoms’ rule]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 8:23 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠הָתֵ֖ם הַ⁠פֹּשְׁעִ֑ים

"when transgressors are complete"

Gabriel is using when transgressors are complete as a common expression of the culture to mean “when sinful people have done all the evil that they will do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when sinful people have finished doing all their evil]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:23 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠פֹּשְׁעִ֑ים

"transgressors"

Some ancient manuscripts read “transgressors.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “transgressions.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

title: Daniel 8:23 (#4)
content:
עַז־פָּנִ֖ים

"strong of face"

Gabriel is using strong of face as a common expression of the culture to mean “fierce and insolent.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [having a fierce and shameless manner]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:23 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠מֵבִ֥ין חִידֽוֹת

"and understanding riddles"

Gabriel is using understanding riddles as a common expression of the culture to mean “skilled at scheming.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and skilled at scheming]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:24 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָצַ֤ם כֹּח⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א בְ⁠כֹח֔⁠וֹ

"And his power will be mighty, but not by his power"

The implication is that this king’s strength will come from a source outside himself, since God will allow him to become powerful. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And his power will be mighty, but the strength will not come from himself]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:24 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִצְלִ֣יחַ וְ⁠עָשָׂ֑ה

"and he will succeed and do"

The phrase succeed and do expresses a single idea. The word succeed tells more about do. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [he will do whatever he wants and be successful at it]

See: Hendiadys

title: Daniel 8:24 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִשְׁחִ֥ית עֲצוּמִ֖ים

"And he will destroy the mighty"

Gabriel is using the adjective the mighty as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And he will destroy powerful people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 8:24 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עַם־קְדֹשִֽׁים

"and the people of the holy {ones"

Gabriel is using the possessive form to describe a people that is characterized by being holy. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the holy people]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 8:25 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עַל־שִׂכְל֗⁠וֹ

"And by his cunning"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of cunning, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And because he acts shrewdly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 8:25 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִצְלִ֤יחַ מִרְמָה֙ בְּ⁠יָד֔⁠וֹ

"he will also make deceit succeed under his hand"

Here, his hand represents “his control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he will also make deceit succeed under his control]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 8:25 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בִ⁠לְבָב֣⁠וֹ יַגְדִּ֔יל

"And in his heart, he will make {himself} great"

Gabriel is using the expression in his heart together with the words that follow as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will become arrogant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will become arrogant]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:25 (#4)
content:
שַׂר־שָׂרִים֙

"the Prince of princes"

The implication is that the Prince of princes is God, who rules over every other ruler. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God, the Prince over all princes]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 8:25 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠אֶ֥פֶס יָ֖ד יִשָּׁבֵֽר

"but he will be broken by no hand"

The expression will be broken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but no hand will break him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 8:25 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠אֶ֥פֶס יָ֖ד יִשָּׁבֵֽר

"but he will be broken by no hand"

Here, hand represents “human power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but he will be broken by no human power]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 8:26 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מַרְאֵ֨ה הָ⁠עֶ֧רֶב וְ⁠הַ⁠בֹּ֛קֶר

"And the appearance of the evening and the morning"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the appearance, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And what was seen concerning the evening and the morning]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 8:26 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר נֶאֱמַ֖ר

"that was told"

The expression was told is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that I told you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 8:26 (#3)
content:
סְתֹ֣ם הֶֽ⁠חָז֔וֹן

"close up the vision"

Gabriel is speaking as if the vision were a document that Daniel could close up, when he means that Daniel should keep its message secret. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [keep the vision secret]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 8:26 (#4)
content:
כִּ֖י לְ⁠יָמִ֥ים רַבִּֽים

"for it is for many days"

Gabriel is using for many days as a common expression of the culture to mean “about a time far in the future.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for it refers to a time far in the future]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:27 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִ֣י דָנִיֵּ֗אל נִהְיֵ֤יתִי

"Then I, Daniel, was finished"

Daniel is using was finished as a common expression of the culture to mean “was completely exhausted.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then I, Daniel, was completely exhausted]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:27 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נֶֽחֱלֵ֨יתִי֙ יָמִ֔ים

"and I was sickened {for} days"

The expression was sickened is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I was ill for days]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 8:27 (#3)
content:
אֶת־מְלֶ֣אכֶת הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ

"the business of the king"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the business, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the king required me to do]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 8:27 (#4)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשְׁתּוֹמֵ֥ם עַל־הַ⁠מַּרְאֶ֖ה

"But I was desolate at the vision"

Daniel is using I was desolate as a common expression of the culture to mean “I was appalled.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But I was appalled by the vision]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 8:27 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֥ין מֵבִֽין

"and not understanding"

Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I was not understanding it]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel - Chapter 9 Introduction
content:
Daniel 9 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

  1. Daniel prays, based on Jeremiah’s prophecy, that God will restore Jerusalem (1–19)
  2. Gabriel comes and explains a further meaning of Jeremiah’s prophecy (20–27)

Translation issues in this chapter

What are the “seventy sevens” that Gabriel describes (9:24)?

The Hebrew word for “seven” can also mean a “week,” that is, a period of seven days, and so some translators say “seventy weeks” here. Some interpreters understand the term in this context to mean a “week of years,” that is, seven years, and so some translations say “490 years.” However, these meanings are not certain. It is also possible that the number seven is being used to symbolize completeness rather than to indicate a specific total of years. So we encourage translators to use general expressions that allow for the range of possible interpretations rather than naming a specific total such as 490. The UST models one way to do this. It translates “seventy sevens” as “seventy sets of seven time periods.”

title: Daniel 9:1 (#1)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת אַחַ֗ת לְ⁠דָרְיָ֛וֶשׁ

"In the year of one to Darius"

The original language uses a cardinal number, one, where your language might use an ordinal number. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as In the year of one to Darius, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the first year of Darius]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 9:1 (#2)
content:
בֶּן־אֲחַשְׁוֵר֖וֹשׁ מִ⁠זֶּ֣רַע מָדָ֑י אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָמְלַ֔ךְ עַ֖ל מַלְכ֥וּת כַּשְׂדִּֽים

"the son of Ahasuerus, from the seed of Madai, who had been made king over the kingdom of the Chaldeans"

Daniel is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See: Background Information

title: Daniel 9:1 (#3)
content:
מִ⁠זֶּ֣רַע מָדָ֑י

"from the seed of Madai"

Daniel is speaking as if Darius were seed that had come from Madai. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a descendant of Madai]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:1 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָמְלַ֔ךְ

"who had been made king"

The expression who had been made king is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [who reigned as king]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:1 (#5)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת אַחַ֗ת לְ⁠דָרְיָ֛וֶשׁ בֶּן־אֲחַשְׁוֵר֖וֹשׁ מִ⁠זֶּ֣רַע מָדָ֑י אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָמְלַ֔ךְ עַ֖ל מַלְכ֥וּת כַּשְׂדִּֽים

"In the year of one to Darius, the son of Ahasuerus, from the seed of Madai, who had been made king over the kingdom of the Chaldeans"

If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine 9:1 and 9:2 into a verse bridge, as the UST does, in order to keep the information about the date of Darius’s reign together.

See: Verse Bridges

title: Daniel 9:2 (#1)
content:
בִּינֹ֖תִי בַּ⁠סְּפָרִ֑ים

"perceived in the scrolls"

The implication is that the scrolls were the writings of the prophets. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [perceived in the sacred scrolls written by the prophets]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:2 (#2)
content:
מִסְפַּ֣ר הַ⁠שָּׁנִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָיָ֤ה דְבַר־יְהוָה֙ אֶל־יִרְמִיָ֣ה הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא לְ⁠מַלֹּ֛אות לְ⁠חָרְב֥וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה

"the number of years that was the word of Yahweh to Jeremiah the prophet for the filling of the desolations of Jerusalem, seventy years"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about seventy years with the information about the number of years. Alternate translation: [the number of years, seventy of them, that was the word of Yahweh to Jeremiah the prophet for the filling of the desolations of Jerusalem]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 9:2 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠מַלֹּ֛אות לְ⁠חָרְב֥וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם

"for the filling of the desolations of Jerusalem"

Daniel is using the filling of the desolations of Jerusalem as a common expression of the culture to mean “the completion of the years during which Jerusalem would lie in ruins.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the completion of the time during which Jerusalem would lie in ruins]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:2 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠חָרְב֥וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם

"the desolations of Jerusalem"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of desolations, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the days in which Jerusalem would lie devastated]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:3 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶתְּנָ֣⁠ה אֶת־פָּנַ֗⁠י אֶל־אֲדֹנָ⁠י֙ הָֽ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים

"And I set my face to the Lord God"

Daniel is using I set my face to the Lord God as a common expression of the culture to mean “I gave my full attention to the Lord God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I turned my full attention to the Lord God]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:3 (#2)
content:
תְּפִלָּ֖ה וְ⁠תַחֲנוּנִ֑ים

"by} prayer and supplications"

The terms prayer and supplications mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [by earnest pleading]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 9:3 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠צ֖וֹם וְ⁠שַׂ֥ק וָ⁠אֵֽפֶר

"with fasting and sackcloth and ashes"

Going without food, wearing rough cloth, and putting ashes on oneself were symbolic actions by which Daniel showed that he was mourning over sin and humbling himself before God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [with fasting and sackcloth and ashes to show that I was mourning and humbling myself]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Daniel 9:3 (#4)
content:
וָ⁠אֵֽפֶר

"and ashes"

In this verse, the word ashes is singular in form, but it refers to all of the particles of ashes as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “ashes.” Alternate translation: [and ash particles]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Daniel 9:4 (#1)
content:
וָֽ⁠אֶתְפַּֽלְלָ֛⁠ה לַ⁠יהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהַ֖⁠י וָ⁠אֶתְוַדֶּ֑ה וָ⁠אֹֽמְרָ֗⁠ה

"And I prayed to Yahweh my God, and I confessed and said"

Daniel is using three verbs, I prayed, I confessed, and said, to introduce a single direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Daniel 9:4 (#2)
content:
אָנָּ֤א אֲדֹנָ⁠י֙

"Oh Lord"

Daniel is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of urgent appeal to God. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Please, Lord]

See: Exclamations

title: Daniel 9:4 (#3)
content:
הָ⁠אֵ֤ל הַ⁠גָּדוֹל֙ וְ⁠הַ⁠נּוֹרָ֔א

"the great and feared God"

The terms great and feared mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the awesome God]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 9:4 (#4)
content:
שֹׁמֵ֤ר הַ⁠בְּרִית֙ וְֽ⁠הַ⁠חֶ֔סֶד

"the one keeping covenant and covenant faithfulness"

The terms keeping covenant and covenant faithfulness mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the one faithfully keeping his covenant]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 9:4 (#5)
content:
הַ⁠בְּרִית֙ וְֽ⁠הַ⁠חֶ֔סֶד

"covenant and covenant faithfulness"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of covenant and faithfulness, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [what he promised, and acting faithfully]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:4 (#6)
content:
לְ⁠אֹהֲבָ֖י⁠ו וּ⁠לְ⁠שֹׁמְרֵ֥י מִצְוֺתָֽי⁠ו

"to the ones loving him and to the keepers of his commandments"

Even though Daniel is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as him and his to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [to the ones loving you and to the keepers of your commandments]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Daniel 9:4 (#7)
content:
לְ⁠אֹהֲבָ֖י⁠ו וּ⁠לְ⁠שֹׁמְרֵ֥י מִצְוֺתָֽי⁠ו

"to the ones loving him and to the keepers of his commandments"

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [to the ones who show that they truly love him by keeping his commandments]

See: Parallelism

title: Daniel 9:5 (#1)
content:
חָטָ֥אנוּ

"we have sinned"

By we, Daniel means himself and his fellow Israelites but not the one to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Exclusive and Inclusive ‘We’

title: Daniel 9:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עָוִ֖ינוּ

"and committed iniquity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and acted perversely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:5 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠ס֥וֹר מִ⁠מִּצְוֺתֶ֖⁠ךָ וּ⁠מִ⁠מִּשְׁפָּטֶֽי⁠ךָ

"turning away from your commandments and your judgments"

Daniel is speaking as if refusing to obey God’s commands were turning away from them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [refusing to obey your commandments and your judgments]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:5 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠מִּצְוֺתֶ֖⁠ךָ וּ⁠מִ⁠מִּשְׁפָּטֶֽי⁠ךָ

"from your commandments and your judgments"

The terms your commandments and your judgments mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [turning away from all of your laws]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 9:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֤א שָׁמַ֨עְנוּ֙ אֶל־עֲבָדֶ֣י⁠ךָ הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֔ים

"And we have not listened to your servants the prophets"

Daniel is using we have not listened to as a common expression of the culture to mean “we have not obeyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And we have not obeyed your servants the prophets]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:6 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֤ר דִּבְּרוּ֙ בְּ⁠שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֔

"who spoke in your name"

Here, your name represents “your authority.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who spoke by your authority]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 9:6 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠אֲבֹתֵ֑י⁠נוּ

"and our fathers"

Daniel is speaking as if all of the earlier generations of the Israelites were their fathers. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and our forefathers]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:7 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠ךָ֤ אֲדֹנָ⁠י֙ הַ⁠צְּדָקָ֔ה

"To you, Lord, {is} righteousness"

Daniel is using this expression as a common expression of the culture to mean “You, Lord, have always done what is right.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You, Lord, have always done what is right]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:7 (#2)
content:
בֹּ֥שֶׁת הַ⁠פָּנִ֖ים

"is} shame of faces"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of shame, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [belong faces that show we are ashamed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:7 (#3)
content:
בֹּ֥שֶׁת הַ⁠פָּנִ֖ים

"is} shame of faces"

Daniel is using faces to represent the whole person who is ashamed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is complete disgrace]

See: Synecdoche

title: Daniel 9:7 (#4)
content:
כַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה

"as this day"

Daniel is using as this day as a common expression of the culture to mean “as is the case at the present time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as is the case at the present time]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:7 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠אִ֤ישׁ יְהוּדָה֙

"to a man of Judah"

In this verse, the word man is singular in form, but it refers to all of the people of Judah as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “man.” Alternate translation: [to the men of Judah]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Daniel 9:7 (#6)
content:
הַ⁠קְּרֹבִ֣ים וְ⁠הָ⁠רְחֹקִ֗ים

"the near and the far"

Daniel is using the adjectives near and far as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the ones who are nearby and the ones who are far away]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 9:7 (#7)
content:
בְּ⁠כָל־הָֽ⁠אֲרָצוֹת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִדַּחְתָּ֣⁠ם שָׁ֔ם

"in all of the lands where you have driven them there"

It might seem that the expression where you have driven them there contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [in all of the lands to which you have driven them]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Daniel 9:8 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠מְלָכֵ֥י⁠נוּ לְ⁠שָׂרֵ֖י⁠נוּ וְ⁠לַ⁠אֲבֹתֵ֑י⁠נוּ

"to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers"

Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to our kings, our princes, and our fathers there is also complete disgrace]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 9:9 (#1)
content:
לַֽ⁠אדֹנָ֣⁠י אֱלֹהֵ֔י⁠נוּ הָ⁠רַחֲמִ֖ים וְ⁠הַ⁠סְּלִח֑וֹת כִּ֥י מָרַ֖דְנוּ בּֽ⁠וֹ

"To the Lord our God, {may there be} compassion and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him"

Even though Daniel is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as the Lord our God and him to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [To you, our Lord and God, we pray for compassion and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against you]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Daniel 9:9 (#2)
content:
הָ⁠רַחֲמִ֖ים וְ⁠הַ⁠סְּלִח֑וֹת

"may there be} compassion and forgiveness"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of compassion and forgiveness, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [we ask that you would act compassionately and forgive us]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:10 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠ק֖וֹל יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֑י⁠נוּ

"to the voice of Yahweh our God"

Here, the voice of Yahweh our God represents “what Yahweh our God commanded.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to what Yahweh our God commanded]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 9:10 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠לֶ֤כֶת בְּ⁠תֽוֹרֹתָי⁠ו֙

"to walk in his laws"

Daniel is speaking as if obeying God’s laws were to walk in them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to obey his laws]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:10 (#3)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָתַ֣ן לְ⁠פָנֵ֔י⁠נוּ

"that he gave to our faces"

Here, our faces represents “us.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [that he gave to us]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 9:10 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠יַ֖ד עֲבָדָ֥י⁠ו הַ⁠נְּבִיאִֽים

"by the hand of his servants the prophets"

Here, the hand represents the agency of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [through his servants the prophets]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 9:11 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תִּתַּ֨ךְ עָלֵ֜י⁠נוּ הָ⁠אָלָ֣ה וְ⁠הַ⁠שְּׁבֻעָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר כְּתוּבָה֙ בְּ⁠תוֹרַת֙ מֹשֶׁ֣ה

"And the oath has been poured out on us, and the curse, that is written in the law of Moses"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the curse with the information about the oath. Alternate translation: [And the oath and the curse have been poured out on us, which are written in the law of Moses]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 9:11 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תִּתַּ֨ךְ עָלֵ֜י⁠נוּ הָ⁠אָלָ֣ה וְ⁠הַ⁠שְּׁבֻעָ֗ה

"And the oath has been poured out on us, and the curse"

Daniel is speaking as if the oath and the curse were a liquid that could be poured out on the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And we have experienced the oath and the curse]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:11 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠תִּתַּ֨ךְ עָלֵ֜י⁠נוּ הָ⁠אָלָ֣ה

"And the oath has been poured out on us"

The expression has been poured out is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And you have poured out the oath]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:11 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֤ר כְּתוּבָה֙

"that is written"

The expression that is written is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that God had written]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:12 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֜קֶם אֶת־דברי⁠ו

"And he has made stand his word"

Daniel is using made stand his word as a common expression of the culture to mean “fulfilled his word.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [kept his word] or [done what he said he would do]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:12 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא־נֶעֶשְׂתָ֗ה תַּ֚חַת כָּל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר נֶעֶשְׂתָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם

"that has not been done under all of the heavens like what has been done to Jerusalem"

The expressions has not been done and has been done are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that he has not done anywhere under all of the heavens like what he has done to Jerusalem]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־חִלִּ֜ינוּ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י ׀ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֗י⁠נוּ

"but we have not entreated the face of Yahweh our God"

Daniel is using the face to represent Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but we have not entreated Yahweh our God himself]

See: Synecdoche

title: Daniel 9:13 (#2)
content:
לָ⁠שׁוּב֙ מֵֽ⁠עֲוֺנֵ֔⁠נוּ

"to return from our iniquities"

Daniel is speaking as if abandoning sin were to return from a place where the people had been. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to turn away from our iniquities] or [to repent of our sin]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:14 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁקֹ֤ד יְהוָה֙ עַל־הָ֣⁠רָעָ֔ה

"And Yahweh watched over the trouble"

Daniel is using Yahweh watched over the trouble as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh kept the disaster ready to send.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh watched for the right time to bring the disaster]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עַתָּ֣ה ׀ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י אֱלֹהֵ֗י⁠נוּ

"And now, Lord our God"

The words And now mark a transition from Daniel’s confession to his request. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [So then, Lord our God]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Daniel 9:15 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠יָ֣ד חֲזָקָ֔ה

"with a mighty hand"

Here, a mighty hand represents “great power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with your mighty strength]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 9:15 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠תַּֽעַשׂ־לְ⁠ךָ֥ שֵׁ֖ם

"and made a name for yourself"

Here, a name represents “a reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and made a reputation for yourself]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 9:16 (#1)
content:
כְּ⁠כָל־צִדְקֹתֶ֨⁠ךָ֙

"according to all of your righteousnesses"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of righteousnesses, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to your righteous deeds]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:16 (#2)
content:
כְּ⁠כָל־צִדְקֹתֶ֨⁠ךָ֙

"according to all of your righteousnesses"

The phrase according to all of your righteousnesses probably refers initially to Yahweh’s “righteous acts,” that is, his acts of deliverance, supremely in the Exodus, described in v. 15. But in light of the overall prayer, it also refers to his righteous character (vv. 7, 14). This phrase could mean: (1) [in keeping with your acts of deliverance] or (2) [because you always do what is right]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:16 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠כָל־צִדְקֹתֶ֨⁠ךָ֙

"according to all of your righteousnesses"

The implication is that your righteousnesses are the righteous deeds by which Yahweh had rescued his people in the past. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [according to all of the righteous deeds by which you have rescued us in the past]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:16 (#4)
content:
יָֽשָׁב־נָ֤א אַפְּ⁠ךָ֙ וַ⁠חֲמָ֣תְ⁠ךָ֔

"may your nose and your heat please turn back"

Daniel is using your nose and your heat as a common expression of the culture to mean “your burning anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you please turn your fierce anger away]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:16 (#5)
content:
הַר־קָדְשֶׁ֑⁠ךָ

"the mountain of your holiness"

Daniel is using the possessive form to describe a mountain that is characterized by holiness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your holy mountain]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 9:16 (#6)
content:
הַר־קָדְשֶׁ֑⁠ךָ

"the mountain of your holiness"

The implication is that the mountain of your holiness is Mount Zion, where the temple stood. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [your holy mountain, Mount Zion]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:17 (#1)
content:
אֶל־תְּפִלַּ֤ת עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֙ וְ⁠אֶל־תַּ֣חֲנוּנָ֔י⁠ו

"to the prayer of your servant and to his supplications"

Even though Daniel is speaking about himself, he refers to himself in the third person as your servant to show humility before God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [listen to my prayer, your servant, and to my supplications]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Daniel 9:17 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָאֵ֣ר פָּנֶ֔י⁠ךָ עַל־מִקְדָּשְׁ⁠ךָ֖ הַ⁠שָּׁמֵ֑ם

"and make your face shine on your desolate sanctuary"

Daniel is speaking as if Yahweh’s favor were light shining from his face onto the sanctuary. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and show your favor to your desolate sanctuary]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:17 (#3)
content:
לְמַ֖עַן אֲדֹנָֽ⁠י

"for the sake of the Lord"

Even though Daniel is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as the Lord to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [for your own sake, my Lord]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Daniel 9:18 (#1)
content:
הַטֵּ֨ה אֱלֹהַ֥⁠י ׀ אָזְנְ⁠ךָ֮ וּֽ⁠שֲׁמָע֒

"Incline your ear, my God, and hear"

Daniel is using Incline your ear as a common expression of the culture to mean “please give me your attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention, my God, and hear]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:18 (#2)
content:
פקח⁠ה עֵינֶ֗י⁠ךָ וּ⁠רְאֵה֙

"Open your eyes and see"

Daniel is using Open your eyes as a common expression of the culture to mean “pay attention.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention and consider]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:18 (#3)
content:
שֹֽׁמְמֹתֵ֔י⁠נוּ וְ⁠הָ⁠עִ֕יר אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָ֥א שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֖ עָלֶ֑י⁠הָ

"our desolations and the city upon which your name is called"

The phrase our desolations and the city upon which your name is called expresses a single idea. The word desolations describes the state of the city. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [the desolations of our city, upon which your name is called] or [the city upon which your name is called, which lies in desolation]

See: Hendiadys

title: Daniel 9:18 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠עִ֕יר אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָ֥א שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֖ עָלֶ֑י⁠הָ

"and the city upon which your name is called"

The expression your name is called is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the city upon which you have put your name]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:18 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠עִ֕יר אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָ֥א שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֖ עָלֶ֑י⁠הָ

"and the city upon which your name is called"

Daniel is using the city upon which your name is called as a common expression of the culture to mean “the city that is your own possession.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the city that is your own possession]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:18 (#6)
content:
מַפִּילִ֤ים תַּחֲנוּנֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ לְ⁠פָנֶ֔י⁠ךָ

"are & making our supplications fall to your face"

Daniel is using making our supplications fall to your face as a common expression of the culture to mean “presenting our requests to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are not laying our petitions before you]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:18 (#7)
content:
רַחֲמֶ֥י⁠ךָ הָ⁠רַבִּֽים

"your great mercies"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of mercies, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how very merciful you are]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:19 (#1)
content:
אֲדֹנָ֤⁠י ׀ שְׁמָ֨עָ⁠ה֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י ׀ סְלָ֔חָ⁠ה אֲדֹנָ֛⁠י הַֽקֲשִׁ֥יבָ⁠ה וַ⁠עֲשֵׂ֖ה

"Lord, hear! Lord, forgive! Lord, pay attention and act"

The words translated as hear, forgive, pay attention and act are imperatives, but they communicate a request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Lord, I ask you to hear! Lord, I beg you to forgive! Lord, I plead with you to pay attention and act]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Daniel 9:20 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠ע֨וֹד אֲנִ֤י מְדַבֵּר֙ וּ⁠מִתְפַּלֵּ֔ל וּ⁠מִתְוַדֶּה֙ חַטָּאתִ֔⁠י וְ⁠חַטַּ֖את עַמִּ֣⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וּ⁠מַפִּ֣יל תְּחִנָּתִ֗⁠י לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהַ֔⁠י עַ֖ל הַר־קֹ֥דֶשׁ אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י

"And I was still speaking and praying and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel and making my supplication fall to the face of Yahweh my God for the mountain of the holiness of my God"

You can create a verse bridge for these two verses, 20–21, in order not to repeat the information “I was still speaking.” The UST models one way to do that.

See: Verse Bridges

title: Daniel 9:20 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠ע֨וֹד אֲנִ֤י מְדַבֵּר֙ וּ⁠מִתְפַּלֵּ֔ל וּ⁠מִתְוַדֶּה֙ חַטָּאתִ֔⁠י וְ⁠חַטַּ֖את עַמִּ֣⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וּ⁠מַפִּ֣יל תְּחִנָּתִ֗⁠י לִ⁠פְנֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהַ֔⁠י עַ֖ל הַר־קֹ֥דֶשׁ אֱלֹהָֽ⁠י

"And I was still speaking and praying and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel and making my supplication fall to the face of Yahweh my God for the mountain of the holiness of my God"

The words that the ULT translates as And I was still speaking indicate that Gabriel came to Daniel at the same time as when Daniel was praying. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [While I was still speaking and praying and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel and presenting my supplication before Yahweh my God for the holy mountain of my God]

See: Connect — Simultaneous Time Relationship

title: Daniel 9:21 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ גַּבְרִיאֵ֡ל אֲשֶׁר֩ רָאִ֨יתִי בֶ⁠חָז֤וֹן בַּ⁠תְּחִלָּה֙

"and the man Gabriel whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning"

Daniel is reintroducing the man Gabriel, whom he had described earlier, as a participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of reintroducing participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and Gabriel, the same man whom I had seen earlier in the vision]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Daniel 9:21 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠אִ֣ישׁ גַּבְרִיאֵ֡ל

"and the man Gabriel"

The implication is that Gabriel was an angel, and Daniel calls him the man because Gabriel appeared in human form. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the angel Gabriel]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:21 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠עֵ֖ת מִנְחַת־עָֽרֶב

"at the time of the offering of the evening"

The implication is that the offering of the evening was the sacrifice that the priests offered every day at that time. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the time when the priests presented the daily evening sacrifice]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:22 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יָּ֖בֶן וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמִּ֑⁠י וַ⁠יֹּאמַ֕ר

"And he made me understand and he spoke with me and said"

Daniel is describing one event, Gabriel making him understand, before describing another event that preceded it, Gabriel speaking with him. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened, as in the UST.

See: Order of Events

title: Daniel 9:22 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠הַשְׂכִּילְ⁠ךָ֥ בִינָֽה

"to make you wise {for} understanding"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of understanding, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to enable you to understand wisely]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:23 (#1)
content:
יָצָ֣א דָבָ֗ר

"a word came forth"

The implication is that a word came forth from God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a word came forth from God]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:23 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִי֙ בָּ֣אתִי

"and I, I have come"

Gabriel is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I have come already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself has come immediately to answer Daniel’s prayer. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I have indeed come]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 9:23 (#3)
content:
כִּ֥י חֲמוּד֖וֹת אָ֑תָּה

"for you {are} desirablenesses"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of desirablenesses, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for you are very precious]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:23 (#4)
content:
כִּ֥י חֲמוּד֖וֹת אָ֑תָּה

"for you {are} desirablenesses"

Gabriel is using the term desirablenesses as a common expression of the culture to mean “one whom God loves greatly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for you are one whom God loves greatly]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:23 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בִין֙ בַּ⁠דָּבָ֔ר וְ⁠הָבֵ֖ן בַּ⁠מַּרְאֶֽה

"So understand the word and understand the appearance"

In the original language, the first understand is “Qal,” and the second understand is from “Hiphil.” The meaning of the second is not to “make understood” but ingressive, to “come to understand.” Some languages may have forms that they can use to express these slightly different meanings. Alternate translation: [So consider this message and grasp the meaning of this vision] or [Therefore, ponder the message and begin to understand the meaning of the vision]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:24 (#1)
content:
שָׁבֻעִ֨ים שִׁבְעִ֜ים נֶחְתַּ֥ךְ

"Seventy sevens have been determined"

The expression have been determined is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God has determined seventy sevens]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:24 (#2)
content:
שָׁבֻעִ֨ים שִׁבְעִ֜ים

"Seventy sevens"

The expression Seventy sevens refers to seventy units of seven. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Seventy periods of seven]

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 9:24 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠כַלֵּ֨א הַ⁠פֶּ֜שַׁע ו⁠ל⁠חתם חטאות וּ⁠לְ⁠כַפֵּ֣ר עָוֺ֔ן וּ⁠לְ⁠הָבִ֖יא צֶ֣דֶק עֹֽלָמִ֑ים

"to finish transgression and to seal up sins and to cover iniquity and to bring in righteousness of eternities"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of transgression, sins, iniquity, and righteousness, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [to stop people from transgressing and to seal up what they have done wrongly and to cover what they have done perversely and to bring in what is eternally right]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 9:24 (#4)
content:
ו⁠ל⁠חתם חטאות

"and to seal up sins"

Gabriel is speaking as if putting an end to sins were to seal up a container so that nothing more could come out of it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to put an end to sins]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:24 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠כַפֵּ֣ר עָוֺ֔ן

"and to cover iniquity"

Gabriel is speaking as if forgiving iniquity were to cover it so that it could no longer be seen. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to forgive iniquity]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:24 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠חְתֹּם֙ חָז֣וֹן וְ⁠נָבִ֔יא

"and to seal up vision and prophecy"

Gabriel is speaking as if bringing about what the prophets foretold were to seal up a document to certify it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to fulfill vision and prophecy]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:24 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לִ⁠מְשֹׁ֖חַ קֹ֥דֶשׁ קָֽדָשִֽׁים

"and to anoint the Holy of Holies"

This could mean: (1) the Holy of Holies refers to the most holy place in the temple or (2) it refers to a most holy person. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and to anoint the most holy place in the temple]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:25 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠תֵדַ֨ע וְ⁠תַשְׂכֵּ֜ל

"And may you know and understand"

The terms know and understand mean similar things. Gabriel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And may you understand this clearly]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 9:25 (#2)
content:
מִן־מֹצָ֣א דָבָ֗ר לְ⁠הָשִׁיב֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠בְנ֤וֹת יְרֽוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙

"from the going forth of the word to return and to build Jerusalem"

Gabriel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [from the time when a king issues the command to return and to build Jerusalem]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 9:25 (#3)
content:
מֹצָ֣א דָבָ֗ר

"the going forth of the word"

The implication is that the going forth of the word is the issuing of a royal decree. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the issuing of the royal decree]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:25 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠הָשִׁיב֙

"to return"

Here return is an idiom meaning “do again.” Alternate translation: [to build Jerusalem again] or [to rebuild Jerusalem]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:25 (#5)
content:
תָּשׁוּב֙ וְ⁠נִבְנְתָה֙

"It will return and it will be built"

As in the instance of “return” earlier in this verse, here It will return and it will be built means “It will be built again.” Alternate translation: [It will be built again] or [It will be rebuilt]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:25 (#6)
content:
שִׁשִּׁ֣ים וּ⁠שְׁנַ֗יִם

"sixty and two"

The expression sixty and two describes a single number. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [sixty-two]

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 9:25 (#7)
content:
תָּשׁוּב֙

"It will return"

The pronoun It refers to Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Jerusalem will return]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 9:25 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠נִבְנְתָה֙ רְח֣וֹב וְ⁠חָר֔וּץ

"and it will be built {with} a square and a trench"

The expression it will be built is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will build it with a square and a trench]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:25 (#9)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠צ֖וֹק הָ⁠עִתִּֽים

"but in distress of times"

Gabriel is using the possessive form to describe times that are characterized by distress. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but in distressful times]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 9:26 (#1)
content:
יִכָּרֵ֥ת מָשִׁ֖יחַ

"the anointed one will be cut off"

The expression will be cut off is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies will cut off the anointed one]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:26 (#2)
content:
יִכָּרֵ֥ת מָשִׁ֖יחַ

"the anointed one will be cut off"

Gabriel is speaking as if the killing of the anointed one were his being cut off, as a branch is cut from a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the anointed one will be killed]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:26 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֣ין ל֑⁠וֹ

"and nothing {will be} to him"

Gabriel is using this expression as a common expression of the culture to mean that the anointed one would be left with nothing. This could mean that he would have (1) no possessions or (2) no one to support him. If this expression does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will have nothing]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:26 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠הָ⁠עִ֨יר וְ⁠הַ⁠קֹּ֜דֶשׁ יַ֠שְׁחִית עַ֣ם נָגִ֤יד הַ⁠בָּא֙

"And the city and the sanctuary, the people of the coming ruler will destroy"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the people of the coming ruler before the information about the city and the sanctuary. Alternate translation: [And the people of the coming ruler will destroy the city and the sanctuary]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 9:26 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠קִצּ֣⁠וֹ בַ⁠שֶּׁ֔טֶף

"And its end {will be} with a flood"

This could mean: (1) its refers to the city or (2) it refers to the coming ruler. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the end of the city will be with a flood]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 9:26 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠קִצּ֣⁠וֹ בַ⁠שֶּׁ֔טֶף

"And its end {will be} with a flood"

Gabriel is speaking as if the destruction that would come were a flood that would sweep everything away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will come to an end in overwhelming destruction]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:26 (#7)
content:
נֶחֱרֶ֖צֶת שֹׁמֵמֽוֹת

"Desolations are determined"

The expression are determined is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God has determined desolations]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 9:27 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִגְבִּ֥יר בְּרִ֛ית לָ⁠רַבִּ֖ים

"And he will strengthen a covenant with many"

This could mean: (1) he refers to the coming ruler or (2) it refers to the anointed one. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And that ruler will strengthen a covenant with many] or [And the anointed one will strengthen a covenant with many]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 9:27 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִגְבִּ֥יר בְּרִ֛ית לָ⁠רַבִּ֖ים

"And he will strengthen a covenant with many"

Gabriel is using strengthen a covenant as a common expression of the culture to mean “make a firm agreement.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will make a firm agreement with many]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 9:27 (#3)
content:
לָ⁠רַבִּ֖ים

"with many"

Gabriel is using the adjective many as a noun to mean a certain group of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [with a large number of people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 9:27 (#4)
content:
זֶ֣בַח וּ⁠מִנְחָ֗ה

"the sacrifice and the offering"

The terms the sacrifice and the offering mean similar things. Gabriel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all the sacrifices]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 9:27 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠עַ֨ל כְּנַ֤ף שִׁקּוּצִים֙

"And on the wing of abominations"

Gabriel is speaking as if abominations were a creature with wings. This could mean: (1) the wing of abominations refers to the highest point of the temple, where something detestable would be set up, or (2) it refers to the extreme degree of the abominations that would be committed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And on the highest point of the temple, detestable things]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 9:27 (#6)
content:
מְשֹׁמֵ֔ם

"will be} something making desolate"

The implication is that something making desolate is a detestable object that would be set up in the temple. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will be placed a detestable object that makes the temple desolate]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 9:27 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠נֶ֣חֱרָצָ֔ה תִּתַּ֖ךְ עַל־שֹׁמֵֽם

"and the thing having been determined will be poured out upon the one desolating"

The expressions having been determined and will be poured out are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God will pour out upon the one desolating what he has determined]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel - Chapter 10 Introduction
content:
Daniel 10 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is the first part of the last section in the book, in which Daniel has a vision and man-like figure appears to him and interprets it.

  1. Narrative introduction to this section (1)
  2. Daniel relates how he had a vision and prayed for three weeks to understand it (2–3)
  3. Daniel relates how a glorious, man-like figure appeared to him (4–9)
  4. The man explains why he was delayed (10–21)

title: Daniel 10:1 (#1)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת שָׁל֗וֹשׁ לְ⁠כ֨וֹרֶשׁ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרַ֔ס

"In the year of three to Cyrus, the king of Persia"

Daniel is using the phrase translated as In the year of three to Cyrus, the king of Persia to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Daniel 10:1 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת שָׁל֗וֹשׁ לְ⁠כ֨וֹרֶשׁ֙

"In the year of three to Cyrus"

Daniel is using the cardinal number three where your language may use an ordinal number. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as three, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the third year of the reign of Cyrus]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 10:1 (#3)
content:
דָּבָר֙ נִגְלָ֣ה לְ⁠דָֽנִיֵּ֔אל

"a word was revealed to Daniel"

The expression was revealed is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God revealed a word to Daniel]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:1 (#4)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖⁠וֹ בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּ֑ר

"whose name was called Belteshazzar"

The expression was called is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whom Babylonian people called Belteshazzar]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:1 (#5)
content:
בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּ֑ר

"Belteshazzar"

The word Belteshazzar is the name of a man. It is the name that the Babylonians gave to Daniel.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 10:2 (#1)
content:
שְׁלֹשָׁ֥ה שָׁבֻעִ֖ים יָמִֽים

"for} three weeks {of} days"

Daniel is using three weeks {of} days as a common expression of the culture to mean “three full weeks.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for three entire weeks]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:3 (#1)
content:
לֶ֣חֶם חֲמֻד֞וֹת לֹ֣א אָכַ֗לְתִּי וּ⁠בָשָׂ֥ר וָ⁠יַ֛יִן לֹא־בָ֥א אֶל־פִּ֖⁠י וְ⁠ס֣וֹךְ לֹא־סָ֑כְתִּי

"I ate no bread of delight, and flesh and wine did not come into my mouth, and anointing, I did not anoint {myself"

Going without bread of delight, and flesh and wine and anointing for three weeks was a symbolic action by which Daniel showed that he was mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [To show that I was mourning, I ate no choice foods or meat or wine, and certainly, I did not anoint myself]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Daniel 10:3 (#2)
content:
לֶ֣חֶם חֲמֻד֞וֹת

"bread of delight"

Daniel is using one kind of food, bread, to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [delightful food]

See: Synecdoche

title: Daniel 10:3 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בָשָׂ֥ר וָ⁠יַ֛יִן לֹא־בָ֥א אֶל־פִּ֖⁠י

"and flesh and wine did not come into my mouth"

Daniel is using flesh and wine did not come into my mouth as a common expression of the culture to mean “I did not eat meat or drink wine.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I did not consume any meat or wine]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:3 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠ס֣וֹךְ לֹא־סָ֑כְתִּי

"and anointing, I did not anoint {myself"

Daniel is repeating forms of the verb anoint in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I did not anoint myself at all]

See: Reduplication

title: Daniel 10:4 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠י֛וֹם עֶשְׂרִ֥ים וְ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֖ה לַ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הָ⁠רִאשׁ֑וֹן

"And on the day of twenty and four to the first month"

Daniel is using the cardinal number twenty and four where your language may use an ordinal number. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as twenty and four, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [And on the twenty-fourth day of the first month]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 10:4 (#2)
content:
לַ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הָ⁠רִאשׁ֑וֹן

"to the first month"

The first month of the Hebrew calendar includes the last part of March and the first part of April on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

See: Hebrew Months

title: Daniel 10:4 (#3)
content:
עַ֣ל יַ֧ד הַ⁠נָּהָ֛ר הַ⁠גָּד֖וֹל

"at the hand of the great river"

Daniel is using at the hand of the great river as a common expression of the culture to mean “on the bank of the great river.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [beside the great river]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:4 (#4)
content:
חִדָּֽקֶל

"the Tigris"

The word Tigris is the name of a river.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 10:5 (#1)
content:
וָ⁠אֶשָּׂ֤א אֶת־עֵינַ⁠י֙ וָ⁠אֵ֔רֶא

"then I lifted up my eyes and saw"

Daniel is using I lifted up my eyes and saw as a common expression of the culture to mean “I looked up and saw.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then I raised my gaze and saw]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה

"and behold"

Daniel is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [there before me]

See: Foreground Information

title: Daniel 10:5 (#3)
content:
אִישׁ־אֶחָ֖ד לָב֣וּשׁ בַּדִּ֑ים

"a man clothed in linen"

Daniel is introducing a man clothed in linen as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [there was a certain man clothed in linen]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Daniel 10:5 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠מָתְנָ֥י⁠ו חֲגֻרִ֖ים בְּ⁠כֶ֥תֶם אוּפָֽז

"and his loins were girded with gold of Uphaz"

The expression were girded is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he had girded his loins with gold of Uphaz]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:5 (#5)
content:
אוּפָֽז

"Uphaz"

The word Uphaz is the name of a place.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 10:6 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠גְוִיָּת֣⁠וֹ כְ⁠תַרְשִׁ֗ישׁ

"And his body {was} like beryl"

The point of this comparison is that just as beryl gleams brightly, so did his body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And his body gleamed as brightly as the gemstone beryl]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 10:6 (#2)
content:
כְ⁠תַרְשִׁ֗ישׁ

"was} like beryl"

A beryl is a kind of precious stone that has a gleaming, greenish color. If your readers would not be familiar with what a beryl is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [was like a gleaming green gemstone]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Daniel 10:6 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠פָנָ֞י⁠ו כְּ⁠מַרְאֵ֤ה בָרָק֙

"and his face {was} like the appearance of lightning"

The point of this comparison is that just as the appearance of lightning is dazzlingly bright, so was his face. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his face was dazzlingly bright, as lightning is]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 10:6 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עֵינָי⁠ו֙ כְּ⁠לַפִּ֣ידֵי אֵ֔שׁ

"and his eyes {were} like torches of fire"

The point of this comparison is that just as torches of fire blaze and glow, so did his eyes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his eyes blazed and glowed as brightly as burning torches]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 10:6 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠זְרֹֽעֹתָי⁠ו֙ וּ⁠מַרְגְּלֹתָ֔י⁠ו כְּ⁠עֵ֖ין נְחֹ֣שֶׁת קָלָ֑ל

"and his arms and his feet {were} like the eye of polished bronze"
