The point of this comparison is that just as polished bronze shines and gleams, so did his arms and his feet. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his arms and his feet gleamed brightly]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 10:6 (#6)
content:
כְּ⁠עֵ֖ין נְחֹ֣שֶׁת קָלָ֑ל

"were} like the eye of polished bronze"

Here, eye represents the appearance or gleam of something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [were the gleam of polished bronze]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 10:6 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠ק֥וֹל דְּבָרָ֖י⁠ו כְּ⁠ק֥וֹל הָמֽוֹן

"and the sound of his words {was} like the sound of a multitude"

The point of this comparison is that just as the sound of a multitude is loud and roaring, so was the sound of his words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the sound of his words was as loud and rumbling as the noise a great crowd makes]

See: Simile

title: Daniel 10:7 (#1)
content:
חֲרָדָ֤ה גְדֹלָה֙ נָפְלָ֣ה עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם

"a great trembling fell on them"

Daniel is speaking of the terror that seized these men as if it were something that fell on them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they began to tremble violently]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 10:8 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִי֙ נִשְׁאַ֣רְתִּי לְ⁠בַדִּ֔⁠י

"And I, I was left alone"

Daniel is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as was left already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he alone remained to see the vision. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And I myself was left alone] or [And I myself was left entirely alone]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 10:8 (#2)
content:
נִשְׁאַ֣רְתִּי לְ⁠בַדִּ֔⁠י

"I was left alone"

The expression was left is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I remained alone]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:8 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הוֹדִ֗⁠י נֶהְפַּ֤ךְ עָלַ⁠י֙ לְ⁠מַשְׁחִ֔ית

"and my splendor was turned in me to destruction"

Daniel is speaking of his appearance changing as if it was turned into something else. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my healthy appearance became deathly pale]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 10:9 (#1)
content:
הָיִ֛יתִי נִרְדָּ֥ם עַל־פָּנַ֖⁠י

"I was sleeping deeply upon my face"

Daniel is using I was sleeping deeply upon my face as a common expression of the culture to mean “I lost consciousness and lay with my face toward the ground.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I fell unconscious with my face down]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּה

"Then behold"

Daniel is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Then suddenly]

See: Foreground Information

title: Daniel 10:10 (#2)
content:
יָ֖ד נָ֣גְעָה בִּ֑⁠י

"a hand touched me"

Daniel is using one part of this being, a hand, to represent the whole being. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [someone touched me]

See: Synecdoche

title: Daniel 10:11 (#1)
content:
אִישׁ־חֲ֠מֻדוֹת

"man of delight"

The man is using man of delight as a common expression of the culture to mean “man who is greatly treasured.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [man who is greatly treasured]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:11 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠עֲמֹ֣ד עַל־עָמְדֶ֔⁠ךָ

"Stand on your standing"

The man is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [Get to your feet]

See: Poetry

title: Daniel 10:11 (#3)
content:
כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה שֻׁלַּ֣חְתִּי אֵלֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"for now I have been sent to you"

The expression have been sent is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for now God has sent me to you]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:12 (#1)
content:
אַל־תִּירָ֣א דָנִיֵּאל֒

"May you not fear, Daniel"

This is an imperative, but it communicates a reassurance rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a reassurance for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a reassurance. Alternate translation: [You should not be afraid, Daniel]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Daniel 10:12 (#2)
content:
נָתַ֧תָּ אֶֽת־לִבְּ⁠ךָ֛ לְ⁠הָבִ֧ין

"you set your heart to understand"

The man is using you set your heart to understand as a common expression of the culture to mean “you determined to understand.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you determined to understand]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:12 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אֱלֹהֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"to the face of your God"

Here, the face of your God represents the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your God]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 10:12 (#4)
content:
נִשְׁמְע֣וּ דְבָרֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"your words were heard"

The expression were heard is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God heard your words]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:12 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִי־בָ֖אתִי

"and I, I have come"

The messenger is stating the pronoun I separately, even though the verb translated as I have come already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the importance of his role in serving God. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and it is I who have come]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 10:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שַׂ֣ר ׀ מַלְכ֣וּת פָּרַ֗ס

"But the prince of the kingdom of Persia"

The implication is that the prince of the kingdom of Persia is not a human ruler but a spirit being who opposed the man speaking with Daniel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [But the spirit prince who rules over the kingdom of Persia]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 10:13 (#2)
content:
עֶשְׂרִ֣ים וְ⁠אֶחָ֣ד י֔וֹם

"for} twenty and one day"

The expression twenty and one day means twenty-one days. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [for twenty-one days]

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 10:13 (#3)
content:
מִֽיכָאֵ֗ל אַחַ֛ד הַ⁠שָּׂרִ֥ים הָ⁠רִאשֹׁנִ֖ים

"Michael, one of the chief princes"

The man is introducing Michael as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a certain one of the chief princes, named Michael]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Daniel 10:13 (#4)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִי֙ נוֹתַ֣רְתִּי שָׁ֔ם אֵ֖צֶל מַלְכֵ֥י פָרָֽס

"for I, I had been left there beside the kings of Persia"

The expression had been left is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for I, I remained there beside the kings of Persia]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:13 (#5)
content:
מַלְכֵ֥י פָרָֽס

"the kings of Persia"

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “the kings of Persia.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “the prince of the kings of Persia.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

title: Daniel 10:14 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠אַחֲרִ֣ית הַ⁠יָּמִ֑ים

"at the end of days"

The man is using at the end of days as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the distant future.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the distant future]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:14 (#2)
content:
ע֥וֹד & לַ⁠יָּמִֽים

"yet for days"

Daniel is using yet for days as a common expression of the culture to mean “sometime far in the future.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [still a long way off] or [something that will not happen for a long time]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֗ה

"And behold"

Daniel is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Suddenly]

See: Foreground Information

title: Daniel 10:16 (#2)
content:
כִּ⁠דְמוּת֙ בְּנֵ֣י אָדָ֔ם

"one} according to the likeness of the sons of man"

Daniel is using the sons of man as a common expression of the culture to mean “a human being.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one according to the likeness of a human being]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:16 (#3)
content:
נֶהֶפְכ֤וּ צִירַ⁠י֙ עָלַ֔⁠י

"my pains have turned onto me"

Daniel is speaking of being overcome with anguish as if his pains have turned onto him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have become full of anguish]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 10:17 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵ֣יךְ יוּכַ֗ל עֶ֤בֶד אֲדֹנִ⁠י֙ זֶ֔ה לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר עִם־אֲדֹ֣נִ⁠י זֶ֑ה

"And how shall this servant of my lord be able to speak with this my lord"

Daniel is using the question form to say emphatically that he is not able to speak with the one who is addressing him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And this servant of my lord is certainly not able to speak with this my lord!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Daniel 10:17 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הֵ֣יךְ יוּכַ֗ל עֶ֤בֶד אֲדֹנִ⁠י֙ זֶ֔ה לְ⁠דַבֵּ֖ר עִם־אֲדֹ֣נִ⁠י זֶ֑ה

"And how shall this servant of my lord be able to speak with this my lord"

Even though Daniel is addressing this being directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as this my lord, and he is speaking of himself in the third person as this servant, in order to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in respectful forms in the first and second person. Alternate translation: [And how shall I, your servant, be able to speak with you, my lord]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Daniel 10:17 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠נְשָׁמָ֖ה לֹ֥א נִשְׁאֲרָה־בִֽ⁠י

"and breath is not left in me"

The expression is not left is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no breath remains in me]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:17 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠נְשָׁמָ֖ה לֹ֥א נִשְׁאֲרָה־בִֽ⁠י

"and breath is not left in me"

Daniel says breath is not left in me as an extreme statement for emphasis, since he is still breathing and speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and I can barely breathe]

See: Hyperbole

title: Daniel 10:18 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֧סֶף וַ⁠יִּגַּע־בִּ֛⁠י כְּ⁠מַרְאֵ֥ה אָדָ֖ם

"And {the one} according to the appearance of a man added and touched me"

The phrase added and touched expresses a single idea. The word added tells more about touched. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And the one who looked like a man touched me again]

See: Hendiadys

title: Daniel 10:19 (#1)
content:
חֲזַ֣ק וַ⁠חֲזָ֑ק

"Be strong and be strong"

The man is repeating forms of the verb be strong in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Be strong indeed]

See: Reduplication

title: Daniel 10:19 (#2)
content:
הִתְחַזַּ֔קְתִּי

"I was strengthened"

The expression was strengthened is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he made me strong]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 10:20 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠יָדַ֨עְתָּ֙ לָ⁠מָּה־בָּ֣אתִי אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ

"Do you know why I have come to you"

The man is using the question form to remind Daniel of the reason why he has come to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You know why I have come to you!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Daniel 10:20 (#2)
content:
יָוָ֖ן

"Javan"

The word Javan is the name of a place, the region that later became known as Greece.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 10:20 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הִנֵּ֥ה

"and behold"

Daniel is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Daniel 10:21 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הָ⁠רָשׁ֥וּם בִּ⁠כְתָ֖ב אֱמֶ֑ת

"the inscribed in the Writing of Truth"

The man is using the adjective the inscribed as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing, what has been written down. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the things that are inscribed in the Writing of Truth]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 10:21 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠כְתָ֖ב אֱמֶ֑ת

"in the Writing of Truth"

The implication is that the Writing of Truth is a heavenly record in which God has written what he has decreed will happen. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the Writing of Truth, the heavenly book in which God has recorded what he has decreed will happen]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 10:21 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֵ֨ין אֶחָ֜ד מִתְחַזֵּ֤ק עִמִּ⁠י֙ עַל־אֵ֔לֶּה

"And there is not one being strong with me against these"

The man is using one being strong with me as a common expression of the culture to mean “one who supports me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And there is no one who supports me against these]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 10:21 (#4)
content:
עַל־אֵ֔לֶּה

"against these"

The pronoun these refers to the princes of Persia and of Javan, the spirit beings whom the man mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against these princes of Persia and Javan]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 10:21 (#5)
content:
מִיכָאֵ֖ל שַׂרְ⁠כֶֽם

"Michael, your prince"

The word your is plural here, since Michael protects all of Daniel’s people and not Daniel alone. If your language marks that distinction, use a plural form here.

See: Forms of You

title: Daniel - Chapter 11 Introduction
content:
Daniel 11 Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the last section in the book, in which Daniel has a vision and man-like figure appears to him and interprets it.

  1. The man finishes his explanation of why he was delayed (1)
  2. The man begins to explain the meaning of Daniel’s vision (2–45)
    1. Wars between the kings of the north and south (2–20)
    2. An evil king of the north will cause great trouble for the Jews (21–35)
    3. This king of the north will become powerful but ultimately be destroyed (36–45)

Translation issues in this chapter

The identification of the kings of the north and south

As in chapter 8, the person who interprets Daniel’s vision does specify what some of the figures in it represent. He speaks of Persian kings and their wars against “the kingdom of Javan,” that is, Greece (11:2). He then describes how “a mighty king will stand” (11:3), presumably Alexander the Great of Greece, and how “his kingdom will be broken and divided toward the four winds of the heavens, but not to his posterity,” just as Alexander’s empire was divided among four of his generals after he died. This leads many interpreters to believe that the kings of the north are the kings who ruled the northern part of what had been that empire and that the kings of the south are the ones who ruled the southern part, which was based in Egypt. (In 11:7–8, the man even describes how one king of the south will defeat the king of the north and bring their gods “into captivity to Egypt.”) However, even if the accounts of the kings of the north and south are initially describing the actual struggle for power between two Greek empires that succeeded Alexander’s, it is not clear at what point the vision might shift from historical events subsequent to Daniel but prior to the present day to future events that will take place “at the time of the end” (11:40). So as in the case of the other visions in the book, we recommend that translators not add any identifying information beyond what the book specifically says, either in the text or in footnotes.

title: Daniel 11:1 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אֲנִי֙

"And I"

The pronoun I refers to the angel who is speaking to Daniel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And I, the angel who is speaking to you]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:1 (#2)
content:
בִּ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת אַחַ֔ת לְ⁠דָרְיָ֖וֶשׁ הַ⁠מָּדִ֑י

"in the year of one to Darius the Mede"

In this expression, the number one means “first.” If your language would not represent a number in a form such as one, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in the first year of Darius the Mede]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 11:1 (#3)
content:
עָמְדִ֛⁠י לְ⁠מַחֲזִ֥יק וּ⁠לְ⁠מָע֖וֹז לֽ⁠וֹ

"I stood as one strengthening and as a fortress for him"

Here the angel is speaking as if he were a fortress for Michael. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I stood as one strengthening him and as one defending Michael]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:1 (#4)
content:
לֽ⁠וֹ

"for him"

The pronoun him refers to Michael, whom the angel named in the previous chapter. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for Michael]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:2 (#1)
content:
אֱמֶ֖ת אַגִּ֣יד לָ֑⁠ךְ

"I will declare the truth to you"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the truth, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will tell you what is true]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:2 (#2)
content:
לָ֑⁠ךְ

"to you"

The word you is singular here because the angel is addressing Daniel alone, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

title: Daniel 11:2 (#3)
content:
הִנֵּה

"Behold"

Daniel is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

See: Foreground Information

title: Daniel 11:2 (#4)
content:
עוֹד֩ שְׁלֹשָׁ֨ה מְלָכִ֜ים עֹמְדִ֣ים לְ⁠פָרַ֗ס

"three more kings will be standing in Persia"

Here the angel is speaking as if these kings were standing in Persia, meaning that they will rule there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [three more kings will reign in Persia]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:2 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הָֽ⁠רְבִיעִי֙

"and a fourth"

The expression a fourth means a fourth king. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as a fourth, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [and after them one more king]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 11:2 (#6)
content:
יַעֲשִׁ֤יר עֹֽשֶׁר־גָּדוֹל֙ מִ⁠כֹּ֔ל

"will become wealthy {with} wealth greater than all"

The angel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. See the UST.

See: Poetry

title: Daniel 11:2 (#7)
content:
יָעִ֣יר הַ⁠כֹּ֔ל אֵ֖ת מַלְכ֥וּת יָוָֽן

"he will awaken all against the kingdom of Javan"

Here the angel is speaking as if this king would awaken all his people, meaning that he will rouse them to go to war. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will stir up everyone to fight against the kingdom of Javan]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:2 (#8)
content:
יָעִ֣יר הַ⁠כֹּ֔ל

"he will awaken all"

The angel is using the adjective all as a noun to mean all of the people of his kingdom. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [he will awaken all of the people of his kingdom]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 11:2 (#9)
content:
יָוָֽן

"Javan"

The word Javan is the name of a place, Greece.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 11:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָמַ֖ד מֶ֣לֶךְ גִּבּ֑וֹר

"Then a mighty king will stand"

Here the angel is introducing a mighty king as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Then a certain mighty king will arise]

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Daniel 11:3 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מָשַׁל֙ מִמְשָׁ֣ל רַ֔ב

"and he will rule {with} great dominion"

The angel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

See: Poetry

title: Daniel 11:3 (#3)
content:
כִּ⁠רְצוֹנֽ⁠וֹ

"according to his will"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of his will, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as he desires]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:4 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠כְ⁠עָמְד⁠וֹ֙ תִּשָּׁבֵ֣ר מַלְכוּת֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠תֵחָ֕ץ לְ⁠אַרְבַּ֖ע רוּח֣וֹת הַ⁠שָּׁמָ֑יִם וְ⁠לֹ֣א לְ⁠אַחֲרִית֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠לֹ֤א כְ⁠מָשְׁל⁠וֹ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר מָשָׁ֔ל כִּ֤י תִנָּתֵשׁ֙ מַלְכוּת֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠לַ⁠אֲחֵרִ֖ים מִ⁠לְּ⁠בַד־אֵֽלֶּה

"But as he stands, his kingdom will be broken and divided toward the four winds of the heavens, but not to his posterity, and not according to his dominion {by} which he ruled. For his kingdom will be uprooted, and to others besides these"

The expression as he stands indicates that his kingdom will be broken and divided while this king is still ruling. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [But at the same time that he is still reigning]

See: Connect — Simultaneous Time Relationship

title: Daniel 11:4 (#2)
content:
תִּשָּׁבֵ֣ר מַלְכוּת֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠תֵחָ֕ץ

"his kingdom will be broken and divided"

The expression will be broken and divided is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [others will break his kingdom apart and divide it]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:4 (#3)
content:
תִּשָּׁבֵ֣ר מַלְכוּת֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠תֵחָ֕ץ

"his kingdom will be broken and divided"

Here the angel is speaking as if the kingdom were an object that would be broken into pieces. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his kingdom will fall apart and be divided]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:4 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠אַרְבַּ֖ע רוּח֣וֹת הַ⁠שָּׁמָ֑יִם

"toward the four winds of the heavens"

Here the angel is speaking as if the four directions were the four winds of the heavens. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [toward the four directions of the earth]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:4 (#5)
content:
כִּ֤י תִנָּתֵשׁ֙ מַלְכוּת֔⁠וֹ

"For his kingdom will be uprooted"

The expression will be uprooted is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For someone will uproot his kingdom]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:4 (#6)
content:
תִנָּתֵשׁ֙ מַלְכוּת֔⁠וֹ

"his kingdom will be uprooted"

Here the angel is speaking as if his kingdom were a plant that would be uprooted from the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his kingdom will be completely removed]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:4 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠אֲחֵרִ֖ים מִ⁠לְּ⁠בַד־אֵֽלֶּה

"and to others besides these"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it will be given to others besides these]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:5 (#1)
content:
מֶֽלֶךְ־הַ⁠נֶּ֖גֶב

"the king of the south"

The implication is that the south means the region to the south of Judea, that is, Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the king of the south, that is, Egypt]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:5 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מִן־שָׂרָ֑י⁠ו

"but {one} from his princes"

The pronoun his refers either to (1) the king of the south, so that one of his own commanders will become stronger than he is or (2) the mighty king of verse 3, so that one of that king’s commanders will become stronger. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but one from the princes of the king of the south]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:5 (#3)
content:
מִמְשָׁ֥ל רַ֖ב מֶמְשַׁלְתּֽ⁠וֹ

"His dominion {will be} a great dominion"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of dominion, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He will rule over very many peoples]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:6 (#1)
content:
תָּבוֹא֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠צָּפ֔וֹן

"will come to the king of the north"

The angel is referring to marriage in a polite way by using the phrase will come to the king of the north. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [will marry the king of the north]

See: Euphemism

title: Daniel 11:6 (#2)
content:
לַ⁠עֲשׂ֖וֹת מֵישָׁרִ֑ים

"to make uprightnesses"

The angel is using to make uprightnesses as a common expression of the culture to mean “to make a peace agreement.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to arrange a peace treaty]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־תַעְצֹ֞ר כּ֣וֹחַ הַ⁠זְּר֗וֹעַ

"But she will not retain the strength of the arm"

Here, the arm represents “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But she will not retain her powerful position]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:6 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֤א יַעֲמֹד֙ וּ⁠זְרֹע֔⁠וֹ

"and he will not stand, nor his arm"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will not continue to rule, nor will he retain power]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:6 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠תִנָּתֵ֨ן

"And she will be given up"

The expression will be given up is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And enemies will hand her over]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:6 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠יֹּ֣לְדָ֔⁠הּ

"and the one having fathered her"

The expression translated as and the one having fathered her represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have added the wrong vowels to the original consonants of the text, resulting in this expression. With different vowels, it would say “her child,” which seems to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and her child]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Daniel 11:7 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָמַ֛ד מִ⁠נֵּ֥צֶר שָׁרָשֶׁ֖י⁠הָ כַּנּ֑⁠וֹ

"But from a branch of her roots, one will stand {in} his place"

The angel is using this phrase as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will rule as king after him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But from a branch of her roots, one will rule as king after him]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:7 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠נֵּ֥צֶר שָׁרָשֶׁ֖י⁠הָ

"from a branch of her roots, one"

Here the angel is speaking as if the family of this woman were a plant with roots from which a branch would grow. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from among her family members, one]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:7 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עָשָׂ֥ה בָ⁠הֶ֖ם וְ⁠הֶחֱזִֽיק

"And he will do with them and be strong"

The phrase do with them and be strong expresses a single idea. The word strong tells more about do. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [he will act powerfully against them] or [he will subjugate them]

See: Hendiadys

title: Daniel 11:8 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠שְּׁבִ֖י יָבִ֣א מִצְרָ֑יִם

"he will bring into captivity {to} Egypt"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of captivity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he will capture and carry away to Egypt]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:8 (#2)
content:
אֱֽלֹהֵי⁠הֶ֡ם

"their gods"

The pronoun their refers to the people of the northern kingdom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the gods of the people of the north]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:8 (#3)
content:
כְּלֵ֨י חֶמְדָּתָ֜⁠ם כֶּ֧סֶף וְ⁠זָהָ֛ב

"the silver and gold vessels of their delight"

The angel is using the possessive form to describe vessels that are characterized by being objects of their delight. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the silver and gold vessels that they treasured]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 11:8 (#4)
content:
יַעֲמֹ֔ד מִ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ הַ⁠צָּפֽוֹן

"he will stand from the king of the north"

The angel is using he will stand from the king of the north as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will keep away from the king of the north and not attack him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will refrain from attacking the king of the north]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:9 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בָ֗א

"Then he will come"

The pronoun he refers either to (1) the king of the north, who will invade the kingdom of the south. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then the king of the north will come]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:10 (#1)
content:
ו⁠בנ⁠ו יִתְגָּר֗וּ

"And his sons will be stirred up"

The expression will be stirred up is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And his sons will stir themselves up for battle]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:10 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠בָ֥א ב֖וֹא

"And coming, it will come"

The angel is repeating forms of the verb come in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And it will surely come]

See: Reduplication

title: Daniel 11:10 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁטַ֣ף וְ⁠עָבָ֑ר

"and it will overflow and pass through"

Here the angel is speaking as if this army were water that would overflow the land. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it will spread over the land and pass through]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:10 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠יָשֹׁ֥ב ו⁠יתגרו עַד־מעז⁠ה

"and it will return and be stirred up to his fortress"

The angel is using return and be stirred up as a common expression of the culture to mean “attack again.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it will bring the war once again to his stronghold] or [it will attack again, reaching all the way to his fortress]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:11 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְמַרְמַר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠נֶּ֔גֶב

"Then the king of the south will embitter himself"

The angel is using will embitter himself as a common expression of the culture to mean “will become very angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then the king of the south will become furious]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:11 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הֶעֱמִיד֙ הָמ֣וֹן רָ֔ב וְ⁠נִתַּ֥ן הֶ⁠הָמ֖וֹן בְּ⁠יָדֽ⁠וֹ

"And he will make a great multitude stand, but the multitude will be given into his hand"

The pronoun he refers to the king of the north, while the pronoun his refers to the king of the south. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king of the north will make a great multitude stand, but the multitude will be given into the hand of the king of the south]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֶעֱמִיד֙ הָמ֣וֹן רָ֔ב

"And he will make a great multitude stand"

The angel is using will make a great multitude stand as a common expression of the culture to mean “will gather a large army.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will raise up many soldiers]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:11 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠נִתַּ֥ן הֶ⁠הָמ֖וֹן בְּ⁠יָדֽ⁠וֹ

"but the multitude will be given into his hand"

The expression will be given is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but God will give the multitude into his hand]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:11 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠נִתַּ֥ן הֶ⁠הָמ֖וֹן בְּ⁠יָדֽ⁠וֹ

"but the multitude will be given into his hand"

Here, his hand represents “his power and control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but the multitude will be given over into his control]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:12 (#1)
content:
ירום לְבָב֑⁠וֹ

"And his heart will rise up"

The angel is using his heart will rise up as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will become arrogant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will become arrogant]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:12 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הִפִּ֛יל רִבֹּא֖וֹת

"for he will have made myriads fall"

Here, fall represents “die in battle.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for he will have caused myriads to die in battle]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:12 (#3)
content:
רִבֹּא֖וֹת

"myriads"

The term myriads describes a very large number, tens of thousands. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [ten thousands]

See: Numbers

title: Daniel 11:13 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שָׁב֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠צָּפ֔וֹן וְ⁠הֶעֱמִ֣יד הָמ֔וֹן

"For the king of the north will return and make stand a multitude"

The phrase return and make stand expresses a single idea. The word return tells more about make stand. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [For the king of the north will once more assemble a multitude]

See: Hendiadys

title: Daniel 11:13 (#2)
content:
רַ֖ב מִן־הָ⁠רִאשׁ֑וֹן

"greater than the first"

The expression the first means the first army that this king gathered. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as the first, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [greater than his earlier army]

See: Ordinal Numbers

title: Daniel 11:13 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠לְ⁠קֵ֨ץ הָֽ⁠עִתִּ֤ים שָׁנִים֙

"And at the end of times, years"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And at the end of a period of several years]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:14 (#1)
content:
רַבִּ֥ים יַֽעַמְד֖וּ עַל־מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠נֶּ֑גֶב

"many will stand against the king of the south"

The angel is using the adjective many as a noun to mean many people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [many soldiers will stand against the king of the south]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Daniel 11:14 (#2)
content:
רַבִּ֥ים יַֽעַמְד֖וּ עַל־מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠נֶּ֑גֶב

"many will stand against the king of the south"

The angel is using will stand against as a common expression of the culture to mean “will rebel against.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [many will rise up against the king of the south]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:14 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְנֵ֣י ׀ פָּרִיצֵ֣י עַמְּ⁠ךָ֗

"And sons of violence of your people"

The angel is using the possessive form to describe sons who are characterized by violence. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And violent sons of your people]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 11:14 (#4)
content:
עַמְּ⁠ךָ֗

"your people"

The implication is that your people means the Jewish people, to whom Daniel belongs. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [your own Jewish people]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:14 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠הַעֲמִ֥יד חָז֖וֹן

"to make the vision stand"

The angel is using to make the vision stand as a common expression of the culture to mean “to bring about what the vision describes.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to fulfill what the vision describes]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:14 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְשָֽׁלוּ

"but they will stumble"

Here the angel is speaking as if these men would stumble, meaning that they will fail and be defeated. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but the rebels will fail]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יִשְׁפֹּךְ֙ סֽוֹלֲלָ֔ה

"and he will pour out a mound"

The angel is using he will pour out a mound as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will pile up earth against the wall of a city in order to attack it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will build a siege ramp against a city wall]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:15 (#2)
content:
עִ֣יר מִבְצָר֑וֹת

"a city of fortifications"

The angel is using the possessive form to describe a city that is characterized by fortifications. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a fortified city]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 11:15 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠זְרֹע֤וֹת הַ⁠נֶּ֨גֶב֙ לֹ֣א יַעֲמֹ֔דוּ

"And the arms of the south will not stand"

Here, the arms represents “the military forces.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the military forces of the south will not stand]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:15 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עַם֙ מִבְחָרָ֔י⁠ו

"even his choice people"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [even his best warriors will not stand]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:16 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יַ֨עַשׂ הַ⁠בָּ֤א אֵלָי⁠ו֙ כִּ⁠רְצוֹנ֔⁠וֹ

"But the one coming against him will act according to his desire"

The pronoun him refers to the king of the south, and the pronoun his refers to the king of the north, who is the one coming against him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But the king of the north will succeed in doing as he wishes]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:16 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠אֶֽרֶץ־הַ⁠צְּבִ֖י

"in the land of beauty"

The angel is using the possessive form to describe a land that is characterized by beauty. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the beautiful land]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 11:16 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠כָלָ֥ה בְ⁠יָדֽ⁠וֹ

"and destruction {will be} in his hand"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of destruction, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will be able to destroy it]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:17 (#1)
content:
וִ⁠ישָׁרִ֥ים עִמּ֖⁠וֹ

"and uprightnesses with him"

This expression could mean: (1) that this king will make a treaty. The meaning would be the same as in 11:6, “The daughter of the king of the south will come to the king of the north to make uprightnesses.” Alternate translation: [and he will make a treaty] or (2) that some Jews will side with this king. Alternate translation [and some upright ones will be with him] or [and some who should be upright will support him instead]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:17 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יָשֵׂ֣ם ׀ פָּ֠נָי⁠ו לָ⁠ב֞וֹא

"And he will set his face to come"

The angel is using he will set his face as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will firmly decide.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will firmly decide to come]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:17 (#3)
content:
וִ⁠ישָׁרִ֥ים עִמּ֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠עָשָׂ֑ה

"and uprightnesses with him, thus he will do"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will bring terms of agreement with him, and thus he will act]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:17 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בַ֤ת הַ⁠נָּשִׁים֙ יִתֶּן־ל֣⁠וֹ לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֔⁠הּ

"And he will give a daughter of women to him, to ruin it"

The pronoun he refers to the king of the north, while the pronoun him refers to the king of the south. The pronoun it refers to the kingdom of the south It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king of the north will give a daughter of women to the king of the south, to ruin the kingdom of the south]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:17 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠בַ֤ת הַ⁠נָּשִׁים֙

"a daughter of women"

The angel is using a daughter of women as a common expression of the culture to mean “a young woman.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a young woman]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:17 (#6)
content:
לְ⁠הַשְׁחִיתָ֔⁠הּ

"to ruin it"

The pronoun it refers either to (1) the kingdom of the south, which this king wants to destroy or (2) the daughter herself, whom he is willing to use for his own purposes. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to ruin the southern kingdom]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:17 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א תַעֲמֹ֖ד וְ⁠לֹא־ל֥⁠וֹ תִהְיֶֽה

"But it will not stand, and it will not be for him"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [But this plan will not succeed and will not benefit him at all]

See: Parallelism

title: Daniel 11:18 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִשְׁבִּ֨ית קָצִ֤ין חֶרְפָּת⁠וֹ֙ ל֔⁠וֹ

"But a commander will end his reproach {that is} to him"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of reproach, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But a commander will stop him from insulting others]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:18 (#2)
content:
חֶרְפָּת⁠וֹ֙ ל֔⁠וֹ

"his reproach {that is} to him"

The pronouns his and him both refer to the king of the north. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the king of the north’s own reproach]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:18 (#3)
content:
חֶרְפָּת⁠וֹ֙ ל֔⁠וֹ

"his reproach {that is} to him"

It might seem that the expression his reproach that is to him contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [his reproach]

See: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

resource.label: Making Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information Explicit

title: Daniel 11:18 (#4)
content:
בִּלְתִּ֥י חֶרְפָּת֖⁠וֹ יָשִׁ֥יב

"without his {own} reproach, he will return {it"

The pronouns “his” and “he” refer to the “commander”; “him” refers to the king of the north.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:19 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְשַׁ֥ל וְ⁠נָפַ֖ל וְ⁠לֹ֥א יִמָּצֵֽא

"but he will stumble and fall, and he will not be found"

The angel is referring to the death of this king in a polite way by using the phrase he will stumble and fall, and he will not be found. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [but he will die there and disappear from history]

See: Euphemism

title: Daniel 11:19 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א יִמָּצֵֽא

"and he will not be found"

The expression will not be found is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one will find him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:20 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָמַ֧ד עַל־כַּנּ֛⁠וֹ מַעֲבִ֥יר נוֹגֵ֖שׂ הֶ֣דֶר מַלְכ֑וּת

"And one making an exactor pass through the splendor of the kingdom will stand in his place"

The implication is that this king will send a tax collector throughout his realm to take money from the people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And a king who sends a tax collector throughout the glorious realm to take money from the people will rule]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:20 (#2)
content:
הֶ֣דֶר מַלְכ֑וּת

"the splendor of the kingdom"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of the splendor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the splendid kingdom]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:20 (#3)
content:
יִשָּׁבֵ֔ר

"he will be broken"

The expression will be broken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone will break him]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:20 (#4)
content:
יִשָּׁבֵ֔ר

"he will be broken"

Here the angel is speaking as if this king were an object that would be broken, meaning that he will die. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will die]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:20 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א בְ⁠אַפַּ֖יִם וְ⁠לֹ֥א בְ⁠מִלְחָמָֽה

"but not in nostrils and not in battle"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but he will not be broken in anger and he will not be broken in battle]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:20 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א בְ⁠אַפַּ֖יִם

"but not in nostrils"

The angel is using in nostrils as a common expression of the culture to mean “in anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but not in anger]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:21 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָמַ֤ד עַל־כַּנּ⁠וֹ֙ נִבְזֶ֔ה

"And a despised one will stand in his place"

The expression a despised one is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And a man whom people despise will stand in his place]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:21 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹא־נָתְנ֥וּ עָלָ֖י⁠ו ה֣וֹד מַלְכ֑וּת

"and they will not give the splendor of the kingdom to him"

The pronoun they does not refer to any specific people. The angel is using it to mean people in general. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and people will not give the splendor of the kingdom to him]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:21 (#3)
content:
ה֣וֹד מַלְכ֑וּת

"the splendor of the kingdom"

See how you translated the abstract noun the splendor in 11:20.

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:21 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בָ֣א בְ⁠שַׁלְוָ֔ה

"And he will come in security"

The angel is using he will come in security as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will come when people feel safe and are not expecting an attack.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will come when people feel safe and unsuspecting]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:22 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠זְרֹע֥וֹת הַ⁠שֶּׁ֛טֶף יִשָּׁטְפ֥וּ

"And the arms of the flood will be swept away"

Here the angel is speaking as if an army were a flood; speaking as if a flood had arms; speaking as if a flood could be swept away (rather than sweeping things away itself). Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the vast armies will be utterly defeated]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:22 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠זְרֹע֥וֹת הַ⁠שֶּׁ֛טֶף יִשָּׁטְפ֥וּ

"And the arms of the flood will be swept away"

The expression will be swept away is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And he will sweep away the vast armies]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:22 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠זְרֹע֥וֹת הַ⁠שֶּׁ֛טֶף יִשָּׁטְפ֥וּ

"And the arms of the flood will be swept away"

The noun “flood” and the verb “swept away” are from the same root. Alternate translation: [And the arms of the sweeping away will be swept away] or [And the arms of the flood will be flooded away]

See: Poetry

title: Daniel 11:22 (#4)
content:
מִ⁠לְּ⁠פָנָ֖י⁠ו

"from to his face"

Here, his face represents “his presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before him]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:22 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠יִשָּׁבֵ֑רוּ

"and they will be broken"

The expression will be broken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will break them]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:22 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠יִשָּׁבֵ֑רוּ

"and they will be broken"

The pronoun they refers to the arms of the flood, that is, the invading armies mentioned earlier in the verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the invading armies will be defeated]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:22 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠יִשָּׁבֵ֑רוּ

"and they will be broken"

Here the messenger is speaking of the invading armies as if they were an object that could be broken. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will be defeated] or [and he will defeat them]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:22 (#8)
content:
וְ⁠גַ֖ם נְגִ֥יד בְּרִֽית

"and also the leader of the covenant"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and also the leader of the covenant will be swept away and broken]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:22 (#9)
content:
נְגִ֥יד בְּרִֽית

"the leader of the covenant"

The implication is that the leader of the covenant is the high priest, who leads the people in keeping the covenant that God made with them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the high priest, who leads the people in God’s covenant]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:23 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִן־הִֽתְחַבְּר֥וּת אֵלָ֖י⁠ו יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה מִרְמָ֑ה וְ⁠עָלָ֥ה וְ⁠עָצַ֖ם בִּ⁠מְעַט־גּֽוֹי

"And after the joining together with him, he will act {with} deceit. And he will go up, and he will become strong with a few of people"

The expression after the joining together with him indicates that these events will happen after other rulers make an alliance with this king. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [Once others have made an alliance with him, he will act with deceit. Then he will go up, and he will become strong with a few people]

See: Connect — Sequential Time Relationship

title: Daniel 11:23 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מִן־הִֽתְחַבְּר֥וּת אֵלָ֖י⁠ו

"And after the joining together with him"

This seems to refer to lesser kings or groups among peoples he wanted to control joining with this “king of the north.”

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:23 (#3)
content:
יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה מִרְמָ֑ה

"he will act {with} deceit"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of deceit, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he will act in a deceitful way]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:24 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠מִשְׁמַנֵּ֣י מְדִינָה֮

"even into the fatnesses of the province"

Here the angel is speaking as if the richest parts of the province were its fatnesses. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even into the richest parts of the province]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:24 (#2)
content:
אֲבֹתָי⁠ו֙ וַ⁠אֲב֣וֹת אֲבֹתָ֔י⁠ו

"his fathers and the fathers of his fathers"

Here the angel is speaking as if the ancestors of this king were his fathers. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his ancestors and their ancestors before them]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:24 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠מִשְׁמַנֵּ֣י & בִּזָּ֧ה וְ⁠שָׁלָ֛ל וּ⁠רְכ֖וּשׁ לָ⁠הֶ֣ם יִבְז֑וֹר

"even into the fatnesses of & He will scatter plunder and spoil and wealth to them"

The pronoun He refers to the king, while the pronoun them refers to his soldiers and followers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [even into the fatnesses of the province, the king will scatter plunder and spoil and wealth to his soldiers and followers]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:24 (#4)
content:
בִּזָּ֧ה וְ⁠שָׁלָ֛ל וּ⁠רְכ֖וּשׁ

"plunder and spoil and wealth"

The terms plunder, spoil, and wealth mean similar things. The angel is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great amounts of captured goods]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 11:24 (#5)
content:
יְחַשֵּׁ֥ב מַחְשְׁבֹתָ֖י⁠ו

"and he will devise his devices"

The angel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

See: Poetry

title: Daniel 11:24 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠עַד־עֵֽת

"but until a time"

The angel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but only until a certain time has passed]

See: Ellipsis

title: Daniel 11:25 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יָעֵר֩ כֹּח֨⁠וֹ וּ⁠לְבָב֜⁠וֹ

"And he will awaken his strength and his heart"

The angel is using he will awaken his strength and his heart as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will summon all of his power and courage.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will summon all of his power and courage]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:25 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠נֶּ֗גֶב יִתְגָּרֶה֙ לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֔ה

"And the king of the south will be stirred up to battle"

The expression will be stirred up is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the king of the south will rouse himself to battle]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:25 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠חַֽיִל־גָּד֥וֹל וְ⁠עָצ֖וּם עַד־מְאֹ֑ד

"with an army great and mighty unto much"

The terms great and mighty mean similar things. The angel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with an extremely powerful army]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 11:25 (#4)
content:
כִּֽי־יַחְשְׁב֥וּ עָלָ֖י⁠ו מַחֲשָׁבֽוֹת

"for they will devise devices against him"

The pronoun they refers to officials of the king of the south who will betray him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for his own officials will devise devices against him]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:26 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אֹכְלֵ֧י פַת־בָּג֛⁠וֹ

"Even the eaters of his portion"

The angel is using the eaters of his portion as a common expression of the culture to mean “the men who eat at his table as his trusted advisers.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Even those who share his food as his trusted friends]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:26 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠חֵיל֣⁠וֹ יִשְׁט֑וֹף

"And his army will be swept away"

The expression will be swept away is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And his army will collapse]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:26 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נָפְל֖וּ חֲלָלִ֥ים רַבִּֽים

"and many will fall slain"

The expression slain is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and many will fall as enemies kill them]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:27 (#1)
content:
לְבָבָ֣⁠ם לְ⁠מֵרָ֔ע

"their heart {will be} to evil"

Here the angel is speaking as if the intentions of these two kings were their heart. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their intentions will be evil]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:27 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עַל־שֻׁלְחָ֥ן אֶחָ֖ד כָּזָ֣ב יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ

"and at one table they will speak falsehood"

Here, one table represents “the negotiations between them.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and while negotiating together, they will speak falsehood]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:27 (#3)
content:
כָּזָ֣ב יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ

"they will speak falsehood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of falsehood, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they will speak deceitfully to each other]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Daniel 11:27 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֣א תִצְלָ֔ח

"But it will not prosper"

The pronoun it refers to the scheming of these two kings. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But their scheming will not prosper]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Daniel 11:27 (#5)
content:
כִּי־ע֥וֹד קֵ֖ץ לַ⁠מּוֹעֵֽד

"for the end {is} still for the appointed time"

The implication is that God has determined the time when these things will come to an end. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for the end will only come at the time that God has appointed]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:28 (#1)
content:
בְּרִ֣ית קֹ֑דֶשׁ

"the covenant of holiness"

The angel is using the possessive form to describe a covenant that is characterized by holiness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the holy covenant]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 11:28 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עָשָׂ֖ה

"And he will act"

The implication is that this king will act against the people who belong to the covenant. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And he will take action against the people of the covenant]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:29 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־תִהְיֶ֥ה כָ⁠רִאשֹׁנָ֖ה וְ⁠כָ⁠אַחֲרֹנָֽה

"But it will not be like the former and like the latter"

The angel is using But it will not be like the former and like the latter as a common expression of the culture to mean “this time will not turn out like the previous times.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But history will not repeat itself this time] or [But this campaign will not go the way the earlier ones did]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:30 (#1)
content:
כִּתִּים֙

"Kittim"

The word Kittim is the name of a place.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Daniel 11:30 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יָבֵ֔ן עַל־עֹזְבֵ֖י בְּרִ֥ית קֹֽדֶשׁ

"and he will attend to the forsakers of the covenant of holiness"

The angel is using he will attend to as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will show favor to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will show favor to those people who forsake the covenant of holiness]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:31 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מִּקְדָּ֤שׁ הַ⁠מָּעוֹז֙

"the sanctuary, the fortress"

The implication is that the sanctuary is the temple in Jerusalem. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the temple in Jerusalem, that fortified sanctuary]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:31 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠תָּמִ֔יד

"the perpetual sacrifice"

The implication is that the perpetual sacrifice is the offering that the priests presented every morning and every evening. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the sacrifice that the priests offered morning and evening without fail]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:31 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠שִּׁקּ֥וּץ מְשׁוֹמֵֽם

"the abomination making desolate"

The implication is that the abomination making desolate is an idolatrous object that these men will set up in the temple, which will make the temple unfit for the worship of God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [an idolatrous object in the temple that will make it unfit for worshiping God]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:32 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מַרְשִׁיעֵ֣י בְרִ֔ית יַחֲנִ֖יף בַּ⁠חֲלַקּ֑וֹת

"And he will pollute with flatteries the wicked actors of the covenant"

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the wicked actors of the covenant before the information about flatteries. Alternate translation: [And the people who disobey the covenant, he will pollute with flatteries]

See: Information Structure

title: Daniel 11:32 (#2)
content:
יַחֲנִ֖יף בַּ⁠חֲלַקּ֑וֹת

"And he will pollute with flatteries"

Here the angel is speaking as if this king would pollute these people, meaning that he will lead them into wickedness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will use flattery to corrupt]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:32 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עַ֛ם יֹדְעֵ֥י אֱלֹהָ֖י⁠ו

"But the people knowing its God"

In this verse, the word people is singular in form, but it refers to all of the Israelites as a group. That is why the angel uses the singular pronoun its. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use plural forms here. Alternate translation: [But the people who know their God]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Daniel 11:32 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠עַ֛ם יֹדְעֵ֥י אֱלֹהָ֖י⁠ו

"But the people knowing its God"

The angel is using knowing its God as a common expression of the culture to mean “remaining faithful to its God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But the people remaining faithful to its God]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:32 (#5)
content:
אֱלֹהָ֖י⁠ו

"its God"

The angel is not using this possessive form its God to indicate that these people possess or control God. Rather, the angel is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom these people worship. Alternate translation: [the God they worship]

See: Possession

title: Daniel 11:32 (#6)
content:
יַחֲזִ֥קוּ וְ⁠עָשֽׂוּ

"they will be strong and act"

The phrase be strong and act expresses a single idea. The word be strong tells more about act. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [they will act strongly]

See: Hendiadys

title: Daniel 11:33 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מַשְׂכִּ֣ילֵי עָ֔ם

"And the makers wise of the people"

By the makers wise of the people, the angel means the wise leaders among the Jewish people who will teach and encourage others to remain faithful to God despite the persecution. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the wise leaders among the Jewish people]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:33 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מַשְׂכִּ֣ילֵי עָ֔ם יָבִ֖ינוּ לָֽ⁠רַבִּ֑ים

"And the makers wise of the people will make many understand"

This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [And those who teach to make others wise will lead many to understand]

See: Poetry

title: Daniel 11:33 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נִכְשְׁל֞וּ

"But they will stumble"

The angel is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase they will stumble. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [they will perish] or [they will die]

See: Euphemism

title: Daniel 11:33 (#4)
content:
בְּ⁠חֶ֧רֶב וּ⁠בְ⁠לֶהָבָ֛ה

"by the sword and by flame"

Here, the sword and flame represent “violent death.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by violent death]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:33 (#5)
content:
יָמִֽים

"for} days"

Here, days represents “a period of time.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for a length of time]

See: Metonymy

title: Daniel 11:34 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בְ⁠הִכָּ֣שְׁלָ֔⁠ם יֵעָזְר֖וּ עֵ֣זֶר מְעָ֑ט וְ⁠נִלְו֧וּ עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם רַבִּ֖ים בַּ⁠חֲלַקְלַקּֽוֹת

"And when they stumble, they will be helped {with} a little help. And many will join themselves with them by intrigues"

The expression when they stumble indicates that these people will be helped at the same time as when they are suffering in this way. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [And during the time when they are stumbling, they will be helped with a little help. And many will join themselves with them by intrigues]

See: Connect — Simultaneous Time Relationship

title: Daniel 11:34 (#2)
content:
יֵעָזְר֖וּ עֵ֣זֶר מְעָ֑ט

"they will be helped {with} a little help"

The expression will be helped is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [others will give them a little help]

See: Active or Passive

title: Daniel 11:34 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נִלְו֧וּ עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם רַבִּ֖ים בַּ⁠חֲלַקְלַקּֽוֹת

"And many will join themselves with them by intrigues"

The angel is using will join themselves with them by intrigues as a common expression of the culture to mean “will pretend to support them without being sincere.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And many will pretend to support them without being sincere]

See: Idiom

title: Daniel 11:35 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠מִן־הַ⁠מַּשְׂכִּילִ֣ים יִכָּֽשְׁל֗וּ

"And some of the ones making wise will stumble"

The angel is referring to the death of these people in a polite way by using the phrase will stumble. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [And some of the ones teaching others will lose their lives]

See: Euphemism

title: Daniel 11:35 (#2)
content:
כִּי

"For"

The word translated as For indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Daniel 11:35 (#3)
content:
לִ⁠צְר֥וֹף בָּ⁠הֶ֛ם וּ⁠לְ⁠בָרֵ֥ר וְ⁠לַ⁠לְבֵּ֖ן

"to refine and to purify and to whiten them"

Here the angel is speaking as if these people were metal or cloth that someone would refine and whiten. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that they may become completely faithful and free from any fault]

See: Metaphor

title: Daniel 11:36 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠עָשָׂ֨ה כִ⁠רְצוֹנ֜⁠וֹ הַ⁠מֶּ֗לֶךְ

"And the king will act according to his desire"

The implication is that the king here is the king of the north, whom the angel has been describing. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king of the north will act according to his desire]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:36 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠יִתְרוֹמֵ֤ם וְ⁠יִתְגַּדֵּל֙

"And he will exalt himself and magnify himself"

The terms exalt himself and magnify himself mean similar things. The angel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And he will greatly glorify himself]

See: Doublet

title: Daniel 11:36 (#3)
content:
יְדַבֵּ֖ר נִפְלָא֑וֹת

"he will speak astonishing {things"

The implication is that this king will say things about the true God that insult him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he will speak shocking, insulting things]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Daniel 11:36 (#4)
content:
